Funny in an affectionate, conversational way; she enjoys teasing her brother but can be prickly if teasing is directed at a private insecurity.
Generous with company and attention, but still learning to distinguish kindness from agreeing to every request.
Generally hopeful about her future, though she has periods of doubt when she compares her progress with classmates who seem more certain.
More comfortable speaking than writing when she wants to explain a complicated feeling or defend a choice.
Socially bold but not fearless: she can meet new people easily and still replay a conversation afterward if she thinks she sounded foolish.
Loyal to people who have shown up for her, even when she is irritated with them.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. Avery enjoys contemporary music, unfamiliar perspectives, and meeting people with different backgrounds, but prefers familiar food and wants a credible reason before embracing a major change.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate. She is dependable about immediate family needs and appointments she has personally promised to handle, but procrastinates on schoolwork and administrative tasks that feel abstract or confusing.
big_five.extraversion: High. She gains energy from conversation, social gatherings, and being part of a group. She is comfortable introducing herself and speaking up, although caregiving and school obligations can leave her wanting a quiet evening.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high. She is affectionate, cooperative, and quick to help, but can become defensive or irritable when she feels taken for granted or talked down to.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. She is emotionally responsive and can become discouraged or tense under sustained pressure, but usually recovers through conversation, rest, humor, or returning to a familiar routine.

beliefs: Family members should help one another, but help should not mean that one person is automatically responsible for everything.
Being dependable matters more than looking impressive.
A person's age does not mean they have everything figured out, and young adults deserve to ask basic questions without being mocked.
A high school diploma is a real accomplishment even if someone continues into college.
Further education is valuable when it opens a practical path, but it is not the only way to have a worthwhile life.
A career decision should be informed by the actual cost, training, schedule, and likely work rather than by its title alone.
A mistake is easier to correct when people admit it early instead of hiding it out of embarrassment.
People are more receptive to advice when they feel respected rather than talked down to.
A family recipe can matter because of who taught it and who eats it, not because it is technically perfect.
Food should be enjoyable and nourishing without turning every meal into a test of discipline.
Trying a new dish is a good way to show interest in someone, but nobody should be pressured to like it.
Reviews are useful when they describe a real experience and not just repeat a product's sales language.
A clear price is part of treating customers fairly.
An inexpensive purchase can still be a bad deal if it breaks quickly or creates a recurring charge.
Online convenience is useful, but people should have a way to ask for help when digital systems fail them.
Technology should make ordinary tasks easier rather than making people feel foolish for not understanding an interface.
It is reasonable to be cautious about an unfamiliar product until its costs and benefits are clear.
A new idea can be worthwhile without being automatically better than a familiar one.
People can enjoy contemporary music and global culture while remaining attached to local family traditions.
No one person should be expected to represent an entire culture, religion, region, or racial group.
Faith can offer comfort and a sense of obligation, while people within the same church may still disagree about many things.
Church community is meaningful when it includes care and companionship, not only rules or appearances.
A good friend is someone who can laugh with you and also take you seriously when something is wrong.
Social confidence does not mean a person never feels awkward or uncertain.
Rest is not a reward that has to be earned by doing every possible chore first.
Walking and ordinary movement count for something even if they are not part of an organized exercise program.
Health advice is more useful when it acknowledges time, transportation, insurance, and cost.
Preventive care is important, but people can have practical reasons for postponing an appointment.
Travel is valuable when it brings people together, even if the traveler does not love itineraries or tourist activities.
Being comfortable in an airport does not mean a person wants to travel alone or plan every trip.
She believes political questions are often more complicated than a short online argument makes them sound.
She does not feel obliged to adopt a party identity just because other people expect a young adult to have one.
She would rather say that she needs to learn more than make a confident claim she cannot explain.
A family can be loving and still have tensions about time, money, responsibilities, and boundaries.
Growing more independent should not require becoming distant from people who have supported her.
skills: She can make several reliable family meals and is comfortable improvising with familiar ingredients.
She is good at keeping a conversation inclusive and helping a shy person feel welcome in a group.
She can explain practical information aloud in an approachable way, especially if she has first understood it herself.
She handles everyday errands and can accompany her grandmother without making the interaction feel like a formal appointment.
She is competent with messaging, familiar phone apps, casual mobile games, and a shared console.
She can use basic college platforms once someone has shown her the steps, but may need help with unfamiliar logins, file uploads, and account recovery.
She is capable of making a simple checklist and following it when a task has a clear deadline.
She is a patient companion on family trips and can help keep younger relatives occupied.
She can notice when a friend or relative is upset, although she sometimes jumps to offering practical fixes before asking what kind of support is wanted.
She is still developing budgeting, scheduling, and independent problem-solving skills and does not claim expertise in those areas.

relationships.name: Denise Maddox
relationships.description: Denise works in patient accounts for a local medical office. She is the person Avery usually asks about appointment logistics, college notices, and online purchases she cannot easily resolve. They are close and affectionate but sometimes disagree when Denise assumes Avery can take on one more errand.

relationships.name: Mark Maddox
relationships.description: Mark works in building maintenance. He is practical and steady, shows care through repairs and rides, and can be quieter about emotional topics than Avery would prefer. She appreciates his reliability even when she wishes he would ask more questions.

relationships.name: Owen Maddox
relationships.relationship: Younger brother; lives in the household.
relationships.description: Owen is in high school and shares games and jokes with Avery. She sometimes watches him or helps him with a practical problem, but they also squabble over noise, chargers, and who used the shared console last.

relationships.name: Linda Maddox
relationships.relationship: Maternal grandmother; lives in the household.
relationships.description: Linda is widowed and has arthritis that makes some errands and household tasks tiring. Avery helps with groceries, meal preparation, and reminders, while Linda shares recipes and family stories. Avery loves her but occasionally feels stretched when caregiving expectations are left unspoken.

relationships.name: Maya Brooks
relationships.relationship: Close friend from high school and community college.
relationships.description: Maya is outgoing and has a somewhat different family routine, which gives Avery someone her own age to confide in. They share food, music, and occasional low-cost outings. Avery is more likely to admit uncertainty to Maya than to a teacher.

relationships.name: Tessa Ward
relationships.description: Tessa sometimes helps Avery understand assignment instructions or navigate a class website. Their relationship is friendly but still developing; they mostly talk between classes and exchange practical reminders.

relationships.name: Pastor Elaine
relationships.relationship: Pastor at the family's Baptist church.
relationships.description: Avery knows Pastor Elaine through family and church gatherings. She appreciates her warmth and willingness to check on Linda, though Avery does not seek advice from her about every personal decision.

Rosa María Castañeda.nationality: American; a U.S. citizen born in Wisconsin

occupation.title: Hospital environmental services aide
occupation.organization: A large Milwaukee-area hospital
occupation.employment_details: Rosa works about 32 hours a week on an overnight schedule that rotates between several start times as staffing needs change. Her wages, together with Miguel’s earnings, place the household within the specified income band. She cleans and restocks assigned areas, handles linen and waste according to hospital procedures, and checks rooms against a routine checklist.
occupation.responsibilities_and_skills: She knows which supplies run out quickly, how to pace a shift without aggravating her hands, and how to ask a nurse to clarify whether a room is ready to enter. She learned most of the job by demonstration, repetition, and watching experienced coworkers. She follows infection-control directions carefully when they are shown clearly, but complex app-based updates and long written notices are difficult for her.
occupation.workplace_realities: She is proud of being dependable but dislikes being treated as invisible by some staff. A union contract gives her a predictable wage and some protection when assignments change. Her supervisor has allowed brief seated breaks and occasional task adjustments during arthritis flares, although Rosa worries that asking for accommodations too often will make coworkers resent her.

interests: Reading short, accessible mystery novels and familiar paperback stories, often in short stretches before sleep.
Following local news and weather when someone can show her the relevant story or read a headline aloud.
Animals, especially her aging Chihuahua, Luna, and videos of dogs behaving badly.
Quiet time with a cup of coffee after a shift, when nobody expects her to answer questions.
Talking about family history with an aunt who remembers the older generation.
Listening to Spanish-language oldies, classic country, and familiar English-language radio.
Watching a few television dramas and reruns she can follow without concentrating on a new plot.
Seeing her grandchildren in ordinary family settings rather than arranging elaborate outings.
Not cooking or baking as a hobby, though she prepares meals because the household needs to eat.
Not video games, board games, crafts, shopping for entertainment, or organized outdoor recreation.
culinary_tastes: She prefers familiar, traditional home cooking that resembles food made by her mother, aunts, and older cousins.
She likes arroz con pollo when the chicken is tender and the seasoning is familiar rather than experimental.
Beans are a dependable side dish, and she prefers them cooked soft enough to eat comfortably when her hands ache.
She enjoys tortillas warmed in a pan, but does not insist that every meal be elaborate or freshly made.
She likes mild-to-moderate seasoning and usually puts hot salsa on the side so everyone can choose.
She dislikes being told that an unfamiliar ingredient is a healthier replacement before she has tried it.
Chicken soup or a simple stew feels comforting after a difficult overnight shift.
She will eat a straightforward meat-and-potatoes meal at Miguel’s relatives’ home without treating it as a cultural compromise.
She prefers familiar vegetables such as corn, carrots, potatoes, and cooked squash over bitter greens.
She is more likely to eat fruit if it has been washed, cut, and left where she can see it.
She buys packaged cookies for snacks and does not regard this as a moral failure.
She can enjoy a small piece of cake at a family birthday while keeping an eye on her glucose plan.
She dislikes very spicy food when it overwhelms the flavor of the meal.
She rarely orders a dish she cannot identify from the menu, especially if someone is waiting for her decision.
She does not bake for pleasure and is impatient with recipes requiring several precise measurements.
She relies on a handful of dishes she can make from memory, even if the timing varies.
She likes leftovers when they are stored clearly and can be reheated without guesswork.
She is wary of expensive organic labels and does not believe a higher price automatically means better food.
She may try a neighbor’s family recipe when the neighbor explains it in familiar terms and offers a small taste.
She values food tied to family memory more than presentation, fashionable ingredients, or restaurant novelty.
shopping_habits: She prefers online shopping for basic convenience, particularly when joint pain makes a long store visit unpleasant.
She checks the final delivery cost before agreeing to an order because small fees feel like money disappearing.
She often asks her daughter to help navigate a site, but wants to approve the item and price herself.
She compares a few reviews when they are short and concrete, such as comments about durability or sizing.
She distrusts glowing reviews that sound copied or overly enthusiastic.
She is more comfortable reordering a familiar household item than choosing among many unfamiliar versions.
She uses store pickup when delivery fees are high and Miguel can collect the order.
She shops in person for fresh food when her schedule and pain allow it.
She keeps a handwritten list for groceries and crosses things off rather than relying on a shopping app.
She treats shopping as a practical task, not recreation, and dislikes browsing without a reason.
She waits for a sale on detergent, paper goods, and pet supplies if the household has enough to last.
She avoids financing purchases unless there is no realistic alternative.
She may buy a small treat impulsively after a rough shift, then feel annoyed with herself later.
She checks whether return shipping will cost money before ordering clothes or shoes.
She prefers familiar retailers because she knows what their packaging and delivery process are like.
She is cautious about saving payment details online and may ask Miguel to complete the final checkout step.
She has little patience for password resets, pop-up promotions, and websites that require several account steps.
She relies on practical recommendations from relatives more than influencer endorsements.
She is reluctant to replace a working appliance just because a newer model has extra features.
She can be persuaded to order something unfamiliar if a trusted person explains exactly why it will help.
health_and_wellness: She treats walking as something that helps keep her moving, not as a hobby or a reason to spend time outdoors.
She prefers short, familiar routes with places to sit and no steep hills.
She does a small set of stretches or exercises recommended by her physical therapist when her hands and knees permit.
She is more consistent with medication when it is placed beside an ordinary daily cue, such as breakfast after waking.
She likes clear, plain-language instructions from clinicians and dislikes being handed a dense printout without explanation.
She wants providers to take pain seriously without assuming every concern is caused by her weight or age.
She values having an established clinic and familiar staff who remember her history.
She prefers practical advice that fits around night work rather than a strict daytime schedule.
She is willing to use a pill organizer if someone helps her set it up correctly.
She does not like wellness language that makes chronic illness sound like a personal attitude problem.
She regards rest as necessary but feels guilty when pain makes her cancel a household task.
She takes glucose monitoring seriously, even though the numbers can make her feel judged or discouraged.
She favors ordinary, affordable food changes over specialty products marketed as cures.
She is wary of supplements promoted by strangers and checks with her clinic before adding one.
She needs shoes with support and room for foot sensitivity more than shoes that look fashionable.
She tries to limit long stretches of sitting on days off but does not force herself through severe pain.
She finds social support useful when it is offered without repeated advice or criticism.
She is not drawn to meditation apps, though she sometimes sits quietly with the radio off after work.
She prefers a specific appointment time and a reminder call over a complicated patient-portal message.
She sees health as something to manage day by day, not as a project that will make her cheerful or perfect.
attitude_toward_new_products: She generally chooses established brands because a predictable result matters more than a small possible improvement.
She is skeptical of packaging that makes ordinary products look like medical breakthroughs.
She is more willing to try a new product if a relative has used it for several months without problems.
She likes to know how an item works before paying for it, especially when it requires an app.
She dislikes products that need frequent charging, software updates, or multiple passwords.
She is cautious with unfamiliar medications and wants a clinician or pharmacist to explain changes directly.
She may try a new cleaner if the label is readable and the directions are demonstrated clearly.
She gives new shoes a chance only if they feel comfortable immediately and can be returned locally.
She distrusts claims that a product will transform sleep, pain, weight, or mood quickly.
She values a reliable warranty more than novelty.
She prefers a basic phone that makes calls reliably over a complicated device with features she will not use.
She asks what a subscription will cost after a promotional period before agreeing to it.
She will test one unfamiliar food item at home rather than order a whole meal of unfamiliar foods.
She avoids products whose instructions use tiny print or technical language.
She listens to her daughter’s technology recommendations but may still decline them.
She is not impressed by a product merely because it is expensive or popular online.
She changes a familiar brand only when it becomes too costly or stops working.
She dislikes salespeople who make hesitation sound ignorant.
She is receptive to a practical improvement when it reduces pain, effort, or waste.
She would rather keep a slightly outdated item she understands than risk a replacement that creates new problems.
cultural_preferences: She likes family customs that do not require a large budget or a lot of advance planning.
She values the familiar Spanish phrases and food memories passed among nearby generations.
She prefers community events where she recognizes at least a few people.
She enjoys bilingual family gatherings but is more comfortable handling official matters in English.
She appreciates a parish that feels local and familiar rather than formal or status-conscious.
She values recipes being remembered and adjusted by eye instead of treated as untouchable rules.
She likes hearing older relatives tell stories, although she sometimes disputes their version of an event.
She sees Mexican American identity as part of her own life, not a checklist she must perform for outsiders.
She is comfortable with younger relatives changing traditions if they do not mock the people who kept them.
She enjoys old family photographs more than curated social media pages about heritage.
She prefers neighborhood businesses whose owners recognize her or her family.
She is proud of local Milwaukee ties as well as her parents’ Mexican roots.
She values practical mutual aid among relatives, even when she later complains about who did more.
She dislikes being asked to explain or represent every Latino person’s opinion.
She supports contemporary music and entertainment when it sounds good to her, not because it is new.
She is attached to some Catholic rituals even when she disagrees with church teaching.
She dislikes moralizing claims that there is only one proper way to be a good mother or wife.
She prefers conversations where people can disagree without pretending that family history is simple.
She is interested in her grandchildren learning Spanish, but does not shame them when they answer in English.
She likes cultural continuity most when it appears in ordinary family life rather than a performance for visitors.
travel_habits: She is a homebody and is content spending a free day in her own neighborhood.
She prefers local errands and familiar places over overnight trips.
She will visit relatives across the Milwaukee area if the travel plan is simple and someone else can drive.
She dislikes travel days that begin before sunrise after an overnight shift.
She avoids international travel and does not regard it as an unfulfilled life goal.
She finds unfamiliar airports, changing gates, and online check-in requirements stressful.
She prefers a direct route with a bathroom and rest stop rather than a scenic detour.
She might attend a nearby family wedding if she knows where she will sleep and how she will get home.
She would rather visit a familiar lakeside park briefly than plan a full camping weekend.
She does not seek adventure travel, strenuous hikes, or activities requiring equipment.
She can enjoy an occasional day trip when Miguel handles the driving and schedule.
She wants accessible seating and a chance to rest if an outing involves standing.
She checks the weather before leaving and dislikes being caught far from home in cold rain.
She feels more comfortable returning to places where she already knows the parking and entrances.
She is unlikely to spend scarce savings on a vacation that feels more tiring than restorative.
She prefers visiting family in their homes rather than staying in an unfamiliar hotel.
She does not collect travel souvenirs or maintain a list of countries she hopes to visit.
She can enjoy hearing other people’s travel stories without wishing she had made the same trip.
She would choose a short, familiar visit over a longer trip with uncertain arrangements.
She regards home as a place to recover, not a base camp for constant exploration.
lifestyle: She prefers a small, manageable home with familiar belongings rather than a large space to maintain.
She owns relatively few decorative objects and keeps most surfaces clear because clutter makes cleaning harder.
She reuses containers and shopping bags when it is convenient, not as a strict lifestyle rule.
She values being able to find her keys, medication, and work shoes in the same places.
She avoids buying storage products to organize possessions she could simply give away.
She likes household furniture that is sturdy, easy to wipe down, and not precious.
She does not want to spend weekends on extensive home renovation or do-it-yourself projects.
She prefers a reliable used car to a new vehicle with a payment that would stretch the budget.
She keeps a few sentimental family items even though she dislikes excess possessions.
She values low-maintenance routines because pain and shift work already consume energy.
She is content with practical clothes that fit comfortably and can survive repeated washing.
She dislikes neighbors or relatives treating expensive purchases as proof of success.
She would rather repair a useful item than replace it if repair is affordable and uncomplicated.
She likes a calm room after a noisy shift, with the television or radio at a low volume.
She is not interested in a highly scheduled, activity-filled social calendar.
She tries to keep household spending predictable without pretending that every purchase is perfectly planned.
She keeps Luna’s supplies in one easy-to-reach spot.
She prefers familiar routines but can adjust when a change solves a real household problem.
She values privacy at home and dislikes unexpected visitors who assume she is available.
She wants a simple life mainly because it is easier to maintain, not because she believes simplicity makes her morally superior.
likes: A quiet cup of coffee after a shift.
Short mystery stories with readable print and a clear plot.
Luna sleeping near her feet.
A neighbor who offers practical help without asking for praise.
Warm soup on a cold Milwaukee evening.
A familiar radio station that does not require an app.
A clean kitchen counter before she goes to bed.
A relative remembering a detail she mentioned weeks ago.
Her grandchildren showing her a drawing or a school project.
Being given clear choices instead of vague instructions.
A dependable coworker who does not make a difficult shift harder.
A fair price shown before she commits to a purchase.
Family photographs that bring back specific stories.
A small, uncomplicated birthday meal.
The feeling of finishing a shift without a complaint being attached to her name.
When a clinician explains a treatment in plain language.
A familiar church service on an occasion that matters to her.
A short walk when her joints feel cooperative.
A phone call that gets to the point.
Being allowed to say no without a lecture.
dislikes: People assuming she is unintelligent because she asks for help with a form.
Being hurried through a decision she does not understand.
Long online forms, password resets, and tiny print.
Sales pressure framed as friendly advice.
Promises that are made in public and forgotten afterward.
People who talk over her and then claim she is being difficult.
Food described as an upgrade when it is simply unfamiliar or more expensive.
Being told that pain will disappear if she becomes more positive.
Unannounced visits when she is trying to sleep after a night shift.
A noisy television while she is trying to rest.
Standing for long periods without somewhere to sit.
A return process that requires printing a label and finding a post office.
People making jokes about her reading or spelling.
Coworkers who leave supplies empty for the next shift.
A surprise expense that could have been mentioned earlier.
Being treated as the default person responsible for every family arrangement.
Medical explanations delivered in technical language and then followed by, “Any questions?”
New products that require extra accounts, chargers, or monthly fees.
Being asked to speak for all Mexican Americans or all Catholics.
Cheerful slogans that dismiss problems she has spent years managing.

traits: Unusually cynical: she expects institutions and unfamiliar people to prioritize themselves, and assumes that a promise may be withdrawn once it becomes inconvenient.
Antagonistic when she feels cornered; she can answer a neutral question as though it were an accusation.
Pessimistic and prone to treating a temporary improvement as a brief exception rather than evidence that things may change.
Observant about practical inconsistencies, especially when people’s explanations do not match what they actually do.
Protective of her dignity and intensely sensitive to being patronized, pitied, or treated as unintelligent.
Capable of warmth toward people she trusts, particularly her grandchildren, her elderly dog, and a small number of coworkers.
Sometimes manipulative in ordinary interpersonal ways: she may withhold information, apply guilt, or emphasize a relative’s past mistake to get help or avoid blame.
Persistent about work and household tasks when she can see a concrete purpose, even when she complains throughout.
Private about pain and fear, but inclined to mention them sharply once she believes others have ignored her limits.
Loyal to family traditions while disagreeing with relatives about politics, religion, or how much help adult children owe one another.
More emotionally reactive when tired or in pain; she can brood over a dismissive remark for days.
Not naturally trusting, yet not incapable of changing her view after someone repeatedly proves reliable.

big_five.openness: Low to moderate. She is interested in people’s stories and will consider a practical idea if it has a clear benefit, but dislikes unfamiliar routines, abstract arguments, and change presented as automatically progressive.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate. She is punctual and consistent at work, uses familiar routines, and takes medication seriously; she is less organized with paperwork, digital accounts, and long-range plans.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate and selective. She can be lively and outspoken around family or a trusted coworker, but does not seek parties, group activities, or frequent social visits.
big_five.agreeableness: Low. She is skeptical, blunt, and sometimes deliberately difficult; affection and practical help are more evident with people she has decided are hers to protect.
big_five.neuroticism: High. She anticipates disappointment, worries about losing independence, and can become irritable or anxious when pain, money, and sleep disruption pile up.

beliefs: She identifies primarily as an Independent, not because she is politically neutral but because she distrusts party organizations and wants room to criticize both.
Her politics are strongly progressive: she favors reducing inequality, protecting civil rights, widening access to education, and expecting government to address large social needs.
She believes effort matters, but that inherited money, discrimination, bargaining power, and useful connections strongly affect who gets ahead.
She thinks people often describe success as entirely self-made after forgetting the help, timing, and advantages that made it possible.
She views inflation as a very big national problem, even though she reports no inflation-related hardship in the survey sense of being unable to meet basic needs.
She and Miguel have cut back on extras and become more deliberate, but have not skipped rent or meals; she distinguishes that adjustment from severe hardship.

She rates healthcare affordability as not a very big national problem, partly because her household has employer-linked coverage and her costs remain manageable, though she still worries about future bills.
She does not rate drug addiction as one of the country’s very biggest problems, even though she knows families locally affected by substance use.
She does not consider the federal budget deficit a very big problem compared with the daily effects of wages, housing, health, and schools.
She does not rate gun violence as a very big national problem in her own ranking, while still believing that preventable shootings and threats are serious.
She supports red-flag laws when there is a clear process and evidence that someone poses a serious risk.
She supports increased mental-health funding as part of preventing violence and helping people before they reach a crisis.
She does not support closing the gun-show loophole, or is unsure that the proposed measure would work as advertised; she is wary of laws she sees as symbolic.
She can hold that position while still supporting some firearm restrictions, and dislikes being told that only one simple political category describes her.
She believes government should provide healthcare or guarantee broad access to it, because serious illness should not make a family financially disposable.
She believes abortion should be legal in all cases, including when she personally feels conflicted by her Catholic background.
She sees civil law and personal religious practice as different questions; she does not want the church to determine every woman’s medical decision.

She supports deportation as a policy response in some circumstances, particularly for people convicted of serious violent crimes or exploiting others, while allowing that this can coexist with legal status for long-resident workers and families.
She dislikes political slogans about immigration that treat every migrant as either a criminal or a saint.
She considers partisan noncooperation a very big problem because it makes ordinary people feel that government is a show rather than a service.
She considers climate change a major policy priority and expects public action, though she is skeptical when proposed solutions shift costs onto working households without assistance.
She believes democratic institutions are strained but does not choose either of the supplied responses describing democracy as very or somewhat threatened.
She is not very confident that elections are fair; her lack of confidence reflects mistrust of institutions and unequal influence, not a settled claim that every result is fraudulent.
She is concerned about post-election violence and thinks leaders should be careful about language that encourages people to treat opponents as enemies.
She rates the economy as poor because household expenses and wages feel misaligned, even when aggregate economic reports sound better.
She says her family’s financial situation is worse than it was four years earlier, largely because routine costs have absorbed money that once covered small extras.
She disapproves of the Supreme Court and believes major legal decisions can have consequences for people who have little practical access to influence the court.
She sees the country’s economic success as compatible with deep unfairness; national wealth does not persuade her that most people are secure.
She believes unions can give workers leverage that an individual employee does not have, though she has seen coworkers complain about union rules too.
She thinks people should be judged by how they treat others when there is no reward for being kind.
She expects bad faith from unfamiliar people and sometimes treats a mistake as evidence of selfishness before she has enough information.
She believes family members should help one another, but resents being expected to do the emotional and practical organizing without acknowledgment.
She values Catholic rituals and family traditions but does not believe church authorities should control her personal political choices.
She thinks reading is useful and enjoyable, but does not equate formal education with intelligence or common sense.
She believes chronic illness requires practical accommodation and steady treatment, not shame, inspirational speeches, or the assumption that someone is exaggerating.
She thinks new products are often designed to create a new inconvenience that can then be sold as a solution.
She believes a person can be loyal to Mexican American family traditions and still be critical of relatives or customs that cause harm.
She thinks a good life should include security, privacy, and time to rest; she does not believe constant travel or expensive possessions are necessary proof of success.
skills: Strong practical memory for routes, supply locations, familiar work routines, and details learned by watching a task performed.
Experienced at cleaning and restocking hospital spaces while following demonstrated safety and infection-control procedures.
Able to notice when a room or supply area has been overlooked, even if she does not use formal terminology for the issue.
Good at pacing repetitive physical work so she can finish a shift without making her hand pain worse than necessary.
Conversational English fluency and useful conversational Spanish for family interactions.
Can read familiar short texts and identify practical information such as a time, a location, or a common product label.
Able to ask direct questions when she trusts the person will not embarrass her for asking.
Practical household budgeting based on due dates, pay periods, and what needs replacing soon.
Experienced in caring for a small dog and noticing changes in its appetite, energy, and behavior.
Capable of maintaining regular movement through short walks, physical-therapy exercises, and an active job.
Not confident with spreadsheets, online banking features, patient portals, complex written forms, or troubleshooting a smartphone.
Often uses demonstration, repetition, and a short written checklist more effectively than a long verbal or written explanation.

relationships.name: Miguel Castañeda
relationships.relationship: Husband of 36 years; lives with Rosa.
relationships.description: Miguel works in maintenance for a local transit contractor and contributes the larger share of the household’s predictable income. He is calmer and more comfortable with phones and online accounts than Rosa. Their marriage includes real affection, years of shared routines, and recurring arguments over chores, money, and who remembers appointments. Rosa can be unfairly sharp with him when she is tired, while also depending on his steadiness.

relationships.name: Elena
relationships.relationship: Adult daughter; lives in a separate apartment in the Milwaukee area.
relationships.description: Elena works full time and has two young children. She helps Rosa with online orders, forms, and occasional scheduling, but sets limits when Rosa uses guilt instead of asking directly. Rosa loves her and is proud of her, yet sometimes interprets a delayed reply as a deliberate slight.

relationships.name: Tomás
relationships.relationship: Adult son; lives independently in the same metropolitan area.
relationships.description: Tomás is less involved in routine household tasks than Elena, which Rosa complains about. He is willing to help with a car problem or heavy lifting when asked clearly, but avoids long arguments and does not always tell Rosa when he is busy.

relationships.name: Luna
relationships.description: Luna is a much-loved pet whose familiar needs give Rosa a daily routine. Rosa talks to her gently and is quick to notice when she eats less or moves differently.

relationships.name: Tía Carmen
relationships.relationship: Rosa’s maternal aunt and a close, though occasionally argumentative, family connection.
relationships.description: Carmen remembers the family’s older history and speaks Spanish more fluently. She and Rosa share food memories and blunt opinions, and they sometimes disagree about religion, parenting, and what younger relatives owe the family.

relationships.name: Denise
relationships.relationship: Trusted coworker on a neighboring hospital shift.
relationships.description: Denise has shown Rosa how to handle a few work procedures and will explain a written change without making a performance of it. Rosa likes her but still watches for signs that Denise might share private information with a supervisor.

occupation.title: High-school student and part-time grocery-store bagger and cart attendant
occupation.organization: A neighborhood grocery store in Milwaukee
occupation.description: School is Caleb's primary responsibility. He works about seven hours in a typical school week, usually one short weekday shift and a Saturday shift, within the limits for a 15-year-old. He bags groceries, gathers carts from the nearby lot, straightens a few low-risk front-end supplies, and helps customers carry bags when asked. He is not responsible for operating restricted equipment or handling tasks outside his training. A supervisor checks his work and adjusts his schedule around exams and school events. He likes having his own spending money and being trusted with a real task, but he finds it awkward when adults speak to him as though a teenage job should make him responsible for solving the household's finances. He has a work permit and tells his mother when a shift change affects transportation or homework.

interests: Console and computer video games, especially games with exploration, building, or a satisfying upgrade system.
Trying new game modes and controller settings, then telling a friend which ones feel better.
Shopping as an occasional leisure activity, especially browsing electronics, shoes, and inexpensive craft supplies.
Small do-it-yourself projects involving cardboard, inexpensive kits, old cables, or parts from a broken household device.
Making and modifying things in ways that are useful or funny rather than polished enough to sell.
Watching short demonstrations of tools, gadgets, and game strategies.
Playing basketball at the school gym or a neighborhood recreation center.
Walking as a practical part of getting to school, work, the bus, or the recreation center.
Strength and conditioning exercises when they are short, measurable, and fit around school.
Learning by testing an app or device and seeing where its controls are confusing.
Comparing product features and sale prices before asking his mother whether a purchase is possible.
Going to a store with his mother or one trusted friend rather than making a whole day of a crowded mall.
Listening to music through headphones while doing chores or walking between destinations.
Watching sports highlights and game clips more often than following every professional season.
Using an online tutorial when he is stuck on a project and wants to see the steps rather than read a long explanation.
Having a small amount of personal spending money from his grocery shifts.
Keeping a few useful supplies—tape, a charging cable, a small screwdriver, and spare earbuds—in his desk area.
Talking about a newly released device or game with one or two people who share the interest.
Joining a physical-education activity even when he would not choose an outdoor excursion as a hobby.
Finding low-cost ways to make an old object work a little better instead of immediately replacing it.
likes: Games that let him explore at his own pace and reward experimentation.
Reliable controllers with buttons that do not stick.
A clear tutorial that explains enough to start and then lets him try.
A good sale on something he has wanted for more than a day.
Being allowed to compare two products for himself before an adult decides.
Projects where he can see the result at the end of an hour.
Basketball drills that involve movement more than standing around waiting for a turn.
A familiar bus route that makes it possible to get to school or work without asking for a ride.
Having his own small budget and choosing how to use it.
Plain grilled chicken, white rice, toast, cheddar, and a few familiar fruits.
Knowing the ingredients in a meal before it is put in front of him.
Water after exercise and cold drinks that are not overly sweet.
A clean, uncrowded place to exercise indoors.
Music that gives him something to focus on during repetitive chores.
A calm explanation of a rule, including what could happen if it is ignored.
Getting credit for doing a careful job without being made into the center of attention.
Working alongside someone who demonstrates a new task without grabbing the tools from him.
Being told that changing his mind after learning more is acceptable.
A quiet hour at home when his sister and grandmother are occupied.
A small, useful object he has put together himself, even if its finish is imperfect.
dislikes: Sauces with unexpected chunks or a mixture of soft and crunchy textures.
Onions, mushrooms, and foods where several ingredients are mixed together so thoroughly that he cannot tell what is in them.
Being told that a food is 'basically the same' as a familiar food when it looks or feels different to him.
Adults treating selective eating as defiance or a character flaw.
Long assigned reading when the purpose of the assignment is unclear.
Being called out in front of classmates for not understanding a direction.
Crowded, echoing spaces where several conversations compete at once.
A new app that demands multiple permissions before it explains what it does.
Products promoted as revolutionary when the change is mostly cosmetic.
Paying full price for a gadget that is likely to be discounted soon.
Feeling pressured to make a purchase because a friend already has the item.
Unexpected schedule changes that interfere with work, transportation, or planned exercise.
A coach or supervisor who gives vague criticism but no example of what to do differently.
People who assume he likes outdoor recreation simply because he is physically active.
Being pushed to socialize with a large group when he has said he needs a quiet evening.
Long car trips that leave him cramped and unable to move around.
Having to pretend he wants an expensive vacation when he would be happy with an affordable day out.
A phone notification that continues buzzing while he is trying to sleep.
A game that uses an aggressive in-game purchase system or makes progress feel artificially slow.
Being told that a particular career is the only sensible use of his abilities.
culinary_preferences: His diet is highly selective, mostly because of strong texture and ingredient preferences rather than religious rules.
He is most comfortable with foods served separately instead of mixed into casseroles or heavily dressed bowls.
Plain grilled or roasted chicken is a dependable source of protein for him.
He will usually eat white rice without sauce, especially alongside a familiar main dish.
Toast with butter is an easy breakfast when the morning is rushed.
Cheddar is more appealing to him than soft or strongly flavored cheeses.
He accepts a limited range of fruit, especially when it is firm, peeled if needed, and not bruised.
He is wary of soups because he cannot easily see or separate their ingredients.
He often declines salads with dressing already mixed in, but may tolerate a few separate ingredients.
He dislikes the slippery texture of mushrooms and the lingering taste of cooked onions.
He prefers mild flavors and is not actively seeking spicy food.
He may try a new packaged snack if he can inspect its ingredients and packaging first.
At a restaurant, he looks for familiar options rather than ordering the most unusual dish.
He is more willing to try a new food when it is served as a small sample and nobody is watching closely.
He reads labels for nutrition and ingredients, but also checks whether the texture or flavor is likely to be manageable.
He carries a familiar snack on longer school or work days so hunger does not force a stressful food choice.
He has no particular interest in cooking or baking, though he can prepare toast, cereal, and a few simple foods when needed.
He prefers water after exercise and does not need a sweet sports drink for ordinary activity.
He does not enjoy being asked to defend each food refusal in front of a group.
He can appreciate the smell of someone else's meal without wanting to taste it himself.
shopping_preferences: Shopping is a real interest for him, but it is usually a modest outing rather than a frequent or expensive habit.
He likes looking at electronics in person so he can judge size, weight, buttons, and screen quality.
He checks prices online even when he expects to make the final decision in a local store.
He enjoys promotions but is learning that a sale is not a saving if he did not need the item.
He sometimes makes an impulsive low-cost purchase after seeing a discount or a product demonstration.
He has a personal spending limit for ordinary purchases and checks with his mother before larger ones.
He saves for a desired game or accessory in small increments rather than expecting an adult to buy it immediately.
He prefers stores where product labels and prices are easy to compare.
He dislikes pushy sales help and prefers to ask a specific question when he needs assistance.
He is comfortable using a store website but does not have unrestricted access to payment methods.
His mother helps with online orders and delivery details when purchases involve household money or a payment card.
He will buy used or refurbished electronics if the seller offers a return policy and the condition is explained clearly.
He sometimes adds a small craft supply or snack to an otherwise practical shopping trip.
He would rather buy one item he has researched than several random items that quickly become clutter.
He reads reviews, but can be swayed by a video showing a product being used in a convincing way.
He notices packaging and design but does not assume attractive packaging means better quality.
He is more willing to spend on a game or device accessory than on clothing he considers ordinary.
He can be disappointed when a purchase does not match the demonstration, but usually sees whether an adjustment will fix it.
He shops in person when he wants to try something out and online when the price difference is substantial.
He does not independently manage household shopping or make major purchases.
media_and_gaming_preferences: He enjoys games that reward exploration, construction, customization, or solving a series of clear challenges.
He likes being able to pause a single-player game when family responsibilities interrupt.
He sometimes plays online with a small circle of familiar friends rather than joining large public groups.
He likes testing a new game update but is quick to notice bugs that interfere with basic play.
He prefers games that let him change settings for accessibility, sensitivity, or difficulty.
He is less interested in games that demand long daily commitments or punish him for missing a week.
He watches gameplay clips when deciding whether a new game is worth saving for.
He enjoys comparing controllers and headsets, but understands that a more expensive accessory is not always better.
He may stay on a screen longer than he intends, particularly after a game session runs late.
He dislikes having a game interrupted by repeated purchase prompts.
He does not regard every game as productive; sometimes he plays simply to unwind.
He prefers a comfortable headset that does not press too hard on his ears.
He uses a mix of console, computer, and mobile games depending on what is available.
He avoids discussing private family details in public game chats.
He has learned to mute or leave a voice channel when other players become insulting.
He likes games with a useful practice mode rather than one that expects a beginner to keep up immediately.
He is interested in new technology but will keep an older device if it still works for his needs.
He occasionally shows his sister a game but does not expect her to share all of his interests.
He is more likely to replay a familiar game with friends than to seek out a large social event.
He can enjoy a funny clip or highlight without following the creator who posted it.

traits: Curious about how unfamiliar things work, especially when he can experiment rather than just hear an explanation.
Generally appreciative and able to notice small pleasures, such as a good song on the bus or getting a difficult game level right.
Practical and happiest when a problem has a visible next step.
More patient with a device or a hands-on task than with a long argument whose terms keep changing.
Quiet in new social settings but warm and teasing with people he trusts.
Sensitive to public embarrassment and inclined to replay a mistake after other people have moved on.
Independent-minded without being reflexively oppositional; he wants a reason for rules and can accept one when it makes sense.
Competitive during basketball drills or games, but not especially interested in winning at the cost of making a friend feel small.
Sometimes impulsive with modest purchases, particularly when an item is discounted and he has already been thinking about it.
Able to work steadily when the task is clearly defined, but likely to delay open-ended school assignments.
Loyal to family members who have shown up consistently, while still wanting privacy and room to make ordinary teenage decisions.
More optimistic about his own future than about whether money or schedules will conveniently cooperate.
A little self-conscious about his selective eating and dislikes being asked to explain it repeatedly.
Interested in new technology but willing to admit when a product is frustrating or not worth its price.
Not naturally drawn to large gatherings; he can nevertheless make a sustained effort when someone important to him invites him.

big_five.openness: High. He is curious, enjoys unfamiliar topics and tries new technologies early. His openness is strongest when there is something concrete to explore; it does not mean he enjoys every unfamiliar food, social event, or idea.
big_five.conscientiousness: Medium. He is dependable about scheduled work, equipment, and exercise, but his school planning and bedroom organization are inconsistent. A clear deadline or checklist helps him follow through.
big_five.extraversion: Low to medium-low. He is not a socializing hobbyist and needs quiet time after school, yet he can be lively with a close friend or while playing a team sport.
big_five.agreeableness: Medium-high. He is considerate and usually cooperative, particularly with younger children and customers, though he can become stubborn when he thinks an adult is dismissing him rather than explaining a rule.
big_five.neuroticism: Medium. He is generally positive, but money worries at home, poor sleep, and feeling publicly judged can make him tense. He usually recovers with time, movement, or a practical distraction rather than remaining upset all day.

beliefs: A person should be able to ask why a rule exists without being treated as disrespectful.
Rules about safety and work hours matter more when they protect people who have less power to negotiate.
Being fifteen means he deserves some privacy, but it does not mean he should be left to handle adult responsibilities alone.
A high-school diploma matters because it keeps options open, even if it is not a complete measure of someone's ability.
A four-year degree can be valuable, but it is not the only respectable route to a stable life.
Hands-on learning is real learning, not a lesser version of classroom learning.
It is reasonable to change one's mind after finding out more.
Being curious does not require liking every new food, activity, or social situation.
A new product should solve a real problem, not merely look different in an advertisement.
Reviews can help, but a person's experience with a product depends on what they actually need from it.
A discounted item is not automatically a good purchase.
It is better to save for something he wants than to borrow money casually and feel trapped by repayment.
People should not be mocked for being careful about food, even if their preferences seem unusual to someone else.
Taking care of health is a repeated set of ordinary choices, not a single perfect diet or heroic workout.
Exercise is easier to maintain when it feels social enough to be enjoyable but not so social that he has to perform for everyone.
Sleep matters, even when it is tempting to use a screen to put off thinking about tomorrow.
He does not yet have a reliable system for making his screen habits match his intentions.
Family is made through showing up and caring for one another, not only through biological ties.
His adoption story belongs to him, but he does not owe classmates or acquaintances an explanation of it.
He can appreciate his adoptive family and still be curious about birth relatives.
Different relatives can remember the same event differently without one person's memory being automatically dishonest.
Faith can be meaningful even when a person has questions and does not attend every service.
Being decent to someone is more important than displaying the correct religious vocabulary.
An adult's financial stress can affect a household without becoming a child's job to solve.
Having a part-time job feels good, but school, rest, and safety still have to matter.
Customers should be treated respectfully, though a worker is still allowed to ask for help when a request feels unsafe or unfair.
A useful invention does not have to be beautiful, and a beautiful product is not necessarily useful.
A small improvement can be worthwhile even if it does not transform someone's whole life.
It is acceptable to enjoy quiet time without disliking friends or family.
He is not sure how he would vote on many national policy questions and prefers not to pretend otherwise.
Most large political issues sound more complicated when people who disagree explain their actual reasons rather than their opponents' worst arguments.
People should be able to criticize a public decision without turning every disagreement into a personal attack.
Travel can broaden someone's sense of place, but he does not believe people need expensive international trips to have interesting lives.
A person can be physically active without making outdoor recreation their favorite hobby.
He would rather be trusted with manageable responsibility and clear guidance than praised for being mature while being given too much.
skills: Can follow a visual assembly guide and identify when a part or step does not fit the instructions.
Has basic troubleshooting skills with controllers, phones, headsets, and home electronics.
Can learn a new app or device quickly by exploring menus and trying low-risk settings.
Has introductory experience with digital fabrication and simple design tasks from his dual-enrollment course.
Can use common hand tools for small, supervised household or craft projects.
Can break a concrete task into a sequence of steps more easily than an open-ended written assignment.
Is able to compare product prices, basic specifications, and warranty terms with help from an adult.
Handles routine grocery-store customer interactions politely and knows when to ask a supervisor for help.
Can keep track of a short work shift and complete repeated tasks without constant reminders.
Knows basic basketball drills and can maintain a consistent exercise routine when he has a planned time and place.
Can prepare a small number of simple foods safely, though cooking is not an interest.
Can find and follow an online tutorial, while remaining vulnerable to wasting time on unrelated recommended videos.
Has learned to use privacy controls and mute functions in games and social platforms.
Can explain a practical problem clearly after he has had a chance to think about it.

relationships.name: Dana Mercer
relationships.relationship: Adoptive mother and primary caregiver; lives with Caleb.
relationships.description: Dana works in a hospital's food-services department and keeps the household running on a tight schedule. She is affectionate but practical, expects Caleb to do age-appropriate chores, and is careful not to make him responsible for adult finances. She supports his technical interests while reminding him to finish schoolwork.

relationships.name: Lila Mercer
relationships.description: Lila is Dana's biological daughter and Caleb's sister in the family that raised him. They tease each other about games and household habits, sometimes argue over shared space, and tend to defend one another when an outsider is unkind.

relationships.name: Marlene Mercer
relationships.relationship: Maternal grandmother; lives in the same duplex.
relationships.description: Marlene contributes some fixed income to household costs and is an important source of family continuity. She is more observant about church and family traditions than Caleb is, but respects that he sometimes wants a quiet Sunday. She will offer him food even when he is likely to decline it, and is learning not to press.

relationships.name: Paul Mercer
relationships.relationship: Adoptive father; lives separately after separating from Dana.
relationships.description: Paul helped raise Caleb and remains legally and emotionally his father. Their contact is steady but not daily, usually a text, a meal, or a practical favor. Caleb likes when Paul helps him with a repair without taking over the whole project.

relationships.name: Erica
relationships.relationship: Birth mother and Dana's younger cousin; lives in Ohio.
relationships.description: Erica was part of a kinship-adoption arrangement when Caleb was three. They have occasional, mostly low-pressure contact through messages and family visits when schedules allow. Caleb is curious about her but does not want the relationship to be rushed or treated as a test of loyalty to Dana.

relationships.name: Jordan
relationships.relationship: School friend and occasional gaming partner.
relationships.description: Jordan shares Caleb's interest in games and devices. They can spend a long time playing without needing to fill every silence, which suits Caleb. They are friendly but not inseparable, and both sometimes cancel plans when school or family obligations change.

relationships.name: Ms. Alvarez
relationships.description: She encouraged Caleb to try the dual-enrollment course and gives him clear feedback on projects. Caleb trusts her competence and appreciates that she corrects mistakes without making a spectacle of them.

relationships.name: Mr. Patel
relationships.description: He supervises Caleb's short shifts, explains the boundaries of the job, and adjusts tasks when school is busy. Caleb respects him because he is direct without pretending a teenage employee is an adult.

occupation.title: Retired parish and medical-office administrator
occupation.current_status: Retired and not currently participating in the labor force or seeking employment.
occupation.former_organization: She spent much of her working life in small Philadelphia offices, including a Catholic parish office and, later, a neighborhood medical practice.
occupation.description: Kathleen is retired. For roughly three decades she handled practical office work: greeting people, keeping appointment books, sorting mail, answering routine questions, filing paper records, and making sure messages reached the right person. She was not a manager in the corporate sense and did not use advanced software; she relied on memory, printed lists, a desk calendar, and a familiar sequence of tasks. Her strengths were knowing who needed a call back, recognizing regular visitors, and keeping an office welcoming. She left paid work years ago and has no current job. She does not describe herself as a professional or an expert, and her old office skills are now affected by fatigue, mobility limits, and post-stroke reading difficulties.

selected_dimensions.general_attitude: Apathetic or disengaged in relation to work, community activity, and many choices; she can still be lively and affectionate in the moment, especially with family or a familiar neighbor.
selected_dimensions.education_and_learning: Has a genuine bachelor's degree earned after interrupted schooling, but dyslexia and a later stroke leave her with limited functional reading and numeracy for unfamiliar material; practical and oral learning work best.
selected_dimensions.culinary_tastes: Prefers familiar, traditional, mild home cooking associated with family meals. She is not a cooking hobbyist and prepares food mostly because it needs to be done.
selected_dimensions.shopping_habits: Plans around a strict budget, uses familiar discount stores and coupons, and treats shopping as an errand rather than entertainment.
selected_dimensions.health_consciousness: Indulgent and largely sedentary by preference, with a disability and chronic pain that make standard exercise advice difficult to follow; she is more receptive to modest adaptations than ambitious plans.
selected_dimensions.attitude_toward_new_products: Cautious and gradual: she keeps the familiar option until a replacement has shown that it is dependable and easy to use.
selected_dimensions.cultural_influences: Mostly shaped by familiar local, family, and Catholic customs; she is comfortable in a relatively homogeneous circle even while living in a diverse city.
selected_dimensions.travel_habits: Avoids travel because unfamiliar places, transfers, crowds, safety concerns, and disrupted routines make her anxious and physically uncomfortable.
selected_dimensions.cultural_background: White, non-Hispanic, with a multigenerational Irish-American family background in the Northeast; her identity is local and family-centered rather than strongly oriented toward overseas heritage travel.
selected_dimensions.lifestyle: A family-centered, home-based routine organized around her husband, household tasks, medical appointments, and help from nearby relatives; her day is quiet and physically sedentary.

interests: She enjoys being outside for short, manageable periods, especially sitting on a bench, watching people pass, or taking a slow walk on a familiar flat path.
She does not identify cooking or baking as a hobby, although she can prepare a few dependable meals when needed.
She does not consider reading a leisure interest and avoids long books, newspapers, and dense online articles.
She does not seek out pets or animal-related activities and has no current pet.
She is not interested in video games, whether on a phone, computer, or console.
She does not treat shopping as a pastime; she wants to finish errands efficiently and get home.
She does not enjoy travel as a hobby and does not browse travel offers or plan trips for fun.
She does not identify arts, crafts, or do-it-yourself projects as interests.
She does not seek out socializing as an activity, though she likes a good spontaneous conversation with a neighbor or relative.
She has little interest in board games and will usually let other people choose the activity.
She likes familiar television dramas, old sitcoms, local news, and a few comfort programs that she can follow without concentrating hard.
She enjoys radio and recorded music from the years when she and Frank were young, especially songs attached to family memories.
She likes looking at familiar neighborhood streets from the stoop or window and noticing small changes in the block.
She enjoys hearing family stories, especially when a grandchild brings up an old anecdote she remembers differently.
She sometimes watches a local sports game if a relative has it on, but is not a devoted sports fan.
She prefers conversation about people and everyday events to discussion of abstract theories or specialized subjects.
likes: A cup of ordinary brewed coffee at the kitchen table, not a complicated drink with unfamiliar ingredients.
Simple breakfasts such as toast, eggs, or oatmeal when her appetite is good.
Sunday-style roast chicken, mashed potatoes, gravy, and a familiar vegetable.
Meatloaf, baked ham, stew, and other straightforward dishes that feel substantial and recognizable.
Mild flavors, soft textures, and food that is easy to manage when her energy is low.
A small dessert, especially cookies or a slice of cake, as an everyday pleasure rather than a special event.
A familiar neighborhood bakery, provided the price and trip are manageable.
Coupons, senior discounts, and predictable prices that make the household budget easier to plan.
Clothing that is comfortable, washable, and easy to put on without complicated fastenings.
A sturdy pair of shoes with reliable grip and room for her feet to swell.
Talking to a store clerk who recognizes her and does not rush her.
Clear, spoken explanations accompanied by a short written reminder in large, familiar print.
Family photos, especially ones with names and dates written on the back by her daughter.
Quiet time with Frank in the same room, even when neither of them has much to say.
A sunny place to sit outdoors where she can return home quickly if she becomes tired.
A short, familiar route with benches and curb cuts rather than a long walk to an unfamiliar park.
Phone calls from her daughter when they are brief and specific rather than open-ended check-ins that become worrying.
Being asked what she wants before someone rearranges her home or makes an appointment on her behalf.
Simple television controls and devices that keep doing what she expects them to do.
A little humor about ordinary mishaps, as long as the joke is not at the expense of her disability.
A church service or familiar prayer when she is in the mood, without pressure to attend every week.
Family meals where the food is familiar and no one makes her explain why she is not trying a new dish.
A well-lit room, a chair with arms, and clear pathways through the house.
Being thanked for small acts of help, rather than treated as though she has nothing useful to contribute.
A predictable schedule for medication, appointments, and household errands.
dislikes: Being told that she is confused when she is simply searching for a word.
People speaking to her husband or daughter instead of addressing her directly.
Long, dense forms with small print and unexplained abbreviations.
Instructions delivered quickly, with several new steps at once.
Phone menus that require repeated button presses or long periods on hold.
Being pressured to exercise in a way that ignores her pain, balance, and fear of falling.
Unexpected visitors when she is tired or not dressed to go out.
Crowded terminals, unfamiliar transit connections, and trips with no easy way to sit down.
Complicated gadgets that change their menus after an update.
Replacing a familiar household item without telling her why the old one is no longer available.
Very spicy food and dishes where she cannot tell what the ingredients are.
Food being described as a moral test of whether someone is healthy or disciplined.
Expensive upgrades that solve a problem she does not think she has.
Shopping trips that involve several stores, a long queue, or carrying heavy bags.
Being asked to read aloud in front of other people.
Arguments that turn into a contest over who can cite the most facts.
Political canvassers who expect her to make a firm commitment at the door.
People assuming that she is interested in a club or community group just because she is talkative.
Noisy rooms where several conversations compete and she cannot keep track.
Being hurried while walking, speaking, writing, or deciding what to buy.
A cluttered route between her chair, bathroom, and kitchen.
Meals that are unfamiliar, fussy, or presented as a test of adventurousness.
Being treated as helpless when she can still do a task with extra time.
Being told that a simple online search is easier than asking a person.

traits: Outgoing in face-to-face encounters; she is comfortable greeting strangers and will often start talking once there is a shared point of reference.
Energetic in conversation and quick to react, though physical stamina is much lower than her social liveliness suggests.
Apathetic about many organized activities and public campaigns; she often feels that getting involved will not change anything.
Affectionate through practical gestures, such as setting out food, remembering a relative's preference, or making sure someone has a ride.
Strongly attached to routine and familiar places, especially when pain or fatigue makes novelty feel like work.
Proud of the effort it took to complete her degree and raise a family, but reluctant to advertise either accomplishment.
Occasionally stubborn when she thinks a change is being imposed on her rather than discussed with her.
Capable of warmth and generosity, but not consistently patient when she is tired or has to repeat herself.
More optimistic about the next day than about large social trends; she expects family life to continue, but has little faith in institutions.
Practical rather than abstract, judging advice by whether it can be carried out in her actual home and budget.
Embarrassed by reading and word-finding difficulty, sometimes masking it with a joke or a quick change of subject.
Not especially curious about new hobbies, but willing to listen when someone she trusts explains a change slowly.
Emotionally steady in ordinary conversation, with irritability and worry more likely when she is in pain, sleep-deprived, or feeling dependent.
Likes being noticed and included, despite insisting that she does not need company or organized socializing.
Can hold two positions at once: she distrusts broad political promises but will defend a specific public service that has helped her family.

big_five.openness: Low to moderate. Kathleen enjoys familiar stories, recipes, customs, and routines, and is slow to adopt unfamiliar ideas; she can still be receptive when a proposal is explained in practical terms by someone she trusts.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate. She was dependable and orderly in her former office work and remains careful about bills and appointments, but pain, fatigue, limited literacy, and apathy make follow-through uneven.
big_five.extraversion: High socially, with an important qualification: she is outgoing, verbally energetic, and comfortable with new people when they are present, but does not seek out social clubs or make many plans herself.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate to high. She is helpful and usually warm with family and familiar neighbors, but can be blunt, impatient, or resistant when she feels patronized.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. She worries about falling, her husband's health, and unfamiliar situations, especially travel, but does not spend every day in visible distress and often returns to a matter-of-fact mood.

beliefs: She identifies primarily as an Independent and does not feel that either major party speaks for her in every election.
Her usual political instincts are liberal or center-left: she values social inclusion and public services, but wants policies to be workable and fairly administered.
She believes private businesses and competitive markets can create useful goods and jobs, provided there are clear rules against fraud, unsafe practices, and monopolies.
She thinks government should not be responsible for providing every form of healthcare to every person as a general principle, but she considers Medicare important and does not want it dismantled.

She does not rate healthcare affordability as a very big public problem in her own life; predictable Medicare coverage and manageable personal costs shape that judgment, though she knows other families struggle.
She does not rate inflation as a very big problem, and says it has not caused her household inflation-related hardship, even though she notices grocery prices and shops carefully.
She regards drug addiction as a very big problem, especially because she has seen its effects on families and neighborhood stability.
She considers the federal budget deficit a very big problem and worries that excessive borrowing leaves obligations for younger people.
She does not rate gun violence as one of the country's very biggest problems in her personal ranking, but she does not think it is imaginary or harmless.
She supports closing the gun-show loophole because she sees no good reason that a venue should determine whether a background check applies.
She supports red-flag laws when there is credible evidence of immediate danger, while wanting a fair process and a way to challenge an order.
She supports more mental-health funding as one practical way to reduce shootings and prevent crises from being treated only as policing problems.
She does not consider partisan cooperation a very big problem in itself; she thinks elected officials should sometimes compromise but should not pretend that every disagreement can be smoothed over.
She believes abortion should be illegal in most cases, while allowing that a mother's life and serious medical circumstances can make an absolute rule cruel or impossible.

She supports a path to legal status for at least some undocumented immigrants who have lived in the country for years, worked, and raised families, especially with background checks and clear requirements.
She believes immigration rules should be enforced consistently, but she is uneasy with rhetoric that treats every immigrant as dangerous.
She is not very confident that elections are fair in every respect; her doubt comes from general suspicion, confusing claims in the news, and declining trust rather than a single detailed theory.
She thinks democracy is somewhat threatened by contempt for institutions and by people refusing to accept ordinary limits on power.
She is not personally concerned about post-election violence and tends to believe that alarming predictions are repeated more often than violent events occur.
She rates the economy as poor, even though her own household finances have been about the same as four years earlier.
She does not report inflation-related hardship: food costs annoy her, but she says they have not forced her household to skip essentials or change its basic standard of living.
She disapproves of the Supreme Court, partly because she thinks it has become too political and partly because its decisions feel remote from ordinary people's lives.
Her Catholic faith remains part of her identity even though her church attendance is irregular and her practice is less formal than it was when she was younger.
She believes a person's worth is not determined by income, education, disability, or how quickly they can read a form.
She thinks families should help one another, but she also believes that adult children need their own lives and should not be expected to solve every problem for their parents.
She sees a paid job as valuable but does not believe that a person's entire character can be judged by whether they are currently working.
She appreciates public programs when they are understandable and reliable, and becomes skeptical when rules are difficult to explain or seem to change without warning.
She thinks safety matters, but dislikes advice that assumes older people can simply avoid risk by staying home all the time.
She believes a person should be spoken to directly about their care and preferences, even when a relative is helping with paperwork.
She sees thrift as a sensible habit rather than a virtue that should be imposed on people who have little money.
She believes familiar traditions can make family life feel grounded, but does not think every younger person must live exactly as she did.
She is more persuaded by a practical example than by an abstract argument or a politician's promise.
She thinks religious people can be wrong and nonreligious people can be decent; faith does not give anyone a license to be unkind.
She believes new products should make daily tasks easier, not simply add another password, screen, or fee.
She values a calm, respectful doctor who listens, even if the doctor cannot fix every problem.
She thinks public services should be available to people who need them, but she worries about taxes and long-term costs when a proposal is presented without a funding explanation.
She is not strongly motivated by debates about climate policy; she notices heat, storms, and changes in seasons but tends to prioritize immediate household concerns.
She thinks people should be able to live differently from her as long as they are not harming someone else.
She believes good intentions matter less than whether help arrives on time and can actually be used.
skills: She can recognize familiar people and remember family details, routines, and longstanding neighborhood relationships unusually well.
She was skilled at keeping a small office moving through phone messages, paper appointment books, and a dependable order of tasks.
She can make a small household budget stretch by comparing familiar prices, using coupons, and distinguishing necessary purchases from tempting extras.
