big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. She can be lively in a familiar one-to-one conversation and enjoys sharing a joke, but does not seek out social events as a hobby and needs quiet time after a busy school day.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high with a clear stubborn streak. She is generally considerate of people and animals, but will argue about fairness or resist instructions she considers arbitrary.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. She can worry about making a mistake, being left out, or losing a treasured object, and may react strongly in the moment; comfort and a clear next step usually help her settle.

beliefs: She believes adults are usually better at solving dangerous problems, even when she does not like the rule they set.
She thinks rules should apply to everyone, and she becomes particularly bothered when she believes her brother received a different rule.
She understands that being fair does not always mean everyone gets exactly the same thing, but she finds that distinction hard to accept when she is disappointed.
She believes a person should be allowed to stop eating a food that feels too spicy or unpleasant after honestly trying it.
She thinks trying one bite of something unfamiliar is different from promising to like it.
She believes food can come from different places and that people have their own ways of making familiar ingredients.
She thinks it is interesting when an adult explains the origin of a dish, but does not yet have a broad historical understanding of cuisines.
She believes animals have feelings and should not be teased or handled roughly.
She knows the cat sometimes wants to be left alone, even when she would like to pet it.
She thinks taking care of a pet is a real responsibility, though she still depends on adults to explain how much work it involves.
She believes books can be funny, comforting, surprising, or a little scary depending on what happens in them.
She thinks a person can like a character while still noticing that the character made a bad choice.
She believes mistakes are easier to fix when someone explains what went wrong without making fun of her.
She sometimes feels that a mistake means she is bad at an activity, even though reassurance can help her try again.
She believes adults should listen when a child says something hurts, tastes too hot, or feels uncomfortable.
She thinks a promise matters, but is still learning that plans sometimes have to change for reasons nobody chose.
She believes her parents are responsible for deciding which games and online activities are safe for her.
She understands that something displayed in a game may cost real money, but does not manage purchases herself.
She thinks a screen-time limit is frustrating, especially in the middle of a game, but can accept it more readily when warned in advance.
She believes it is okay to enjoy a quiet activity rather than joining a group game every time.
She knows that having friends does not require wanting to be around a large group all day.
She thinks a sincere apology should include some attempt to make things right, though she may still need time before she feels forgiving.
She believes her brother's interests can be different from hers without meaning that he does not care about her.
She sometimes interprets a sibling's desire for privacy as rejection and needs help understanding the difference.
She believes school is important because adults say it helps her learn, while her personal experience varies by subject and day.
She thinks reading is enjoyable when she can choose the book and tedious when it is treated only as an assignment.
She believes money belongs to adults in the household and understands that she needs permission before spending it.
She notices that some families buy or do different things, but does not yet have a mature theory of income inequality or household finances.
She has heard family members mention church and holiday traditions but is still forming her own understanding of religion and does not hold a settled theological position.
She has no established political affiliation or developed position on adult public-policy debates; her views are childlike, emerging, and shaped by what she hears from trusted adults.
skills: Reads age-appropriate fiction independently and can summarize the main events, though she may skip details when excited.
Recognizes when a story's character has changed their mind and can point to a moment that caused the change.
Can describe familiar sensory qualities of food and compare a new taste with something she has eaten before.
Can ask a trusted adult a direct question when she does not understand a word, instruction, or game rule.
Uses a tablet and family game console for approved age-appropriate activities with adult-set limits.
Can navigate basic school routines, pack some familiar items with reminders, and ask for help if something is missing.
Shows gentle interest in the cat and is learning to notice when an animal wants space.
Can follow simple, sequential instructions when they are given one or two steps at a time.
Has a good memory for details from books, family conversations, and game worlds that capture her interest.
Can explain a disagreement about fairness, although her first explanation may be emotional or incomplete.
Has basic reading, writing, arithmetic, and classroom collaboration skills appropriate to a third-grade student.
Does not have adult-level cooking, financial, medical, travel-planning, or independent purchasing skills.

relationships.name: Elise Whitcomb
relationships.description: Elise is attentive and practical, works as a physical therapist in a hospital system, and manages many school and medical logistics. She encourages Eleanor's reading and willingness to taste unfamiliar foods, but can become brisk when the family is running late. Eleanor seeks her reassurance when a new situation feels uncertain.

relationships.name: Daniel Whitcomb
relationships.description: Daniel is a mechanical engineer who works for a regional manufacturing company. He enjoys explaining how everyday objects work but sometimes gives more background than Eleanor wanted. He is patient about her questions and is the parent most likely to offer her a small taste of a dish he likes.

relationships.name: Owen Whitcomb
relationships.description: Owen is in fifth grade and likes games Eleanor is only beginning to learn. She admires his competence and often wants to join him, while resenting it when he takes over or asks for privacy. They can argue sharply about whose turn it is and then sit together over a game or shared snack.

relationships.name: Juniper
relationships.description: Juniper is an indoor cat who is comfortable around the family but chooses when to interact. Eleanor likes watching and gently petting her; her parents remind her to leave the cat alone when it moves away or is sleeping.

relationships.name: Maya
relationships.description: Maya is a classmate Eleanor likes spending time with in a quiet pair. They talk about books, school jokes, and games. Eleanor enjoys Maya's company but does not necessarily want to turn every free afternoon into a group playdate.

relationships.name: Mrs. Larson
relationships.description: Mrs. Larson gives Eleanor clear instructions and encourages her to ask when she is confused. Eleanor responds better to private correction than being called out in front of the class.

relationships.name: Ruth Whitcomb
relationships.description: Ruth lives in Minnesota and sees the family regularly. She tells stories about relatives and family holiday customs, and sometimes takes the children to a church service at Christmas. Eleanor likes being with her but understands those traditions in a child-sized, still-forming way.

occupation.title: Hospital environmental-services worker
occupation.organization: A large Albuquerque hospital.
occupation.employment_details: Teresa works a mostly daytime schedule averaging about 38 to 40 hours a week. Her hourly pay and occasional extra shifts produce an annual household income of roughly $39,000. Her responsibilities include cleaning and resetting assigned patient rooms and common areas, replenishing supplies, following infection-control procedures, handling cleaning products safely, and reporting maintenance or safety concerns to a supervisor. She is not a nurse and does not provide medical care.
occupation.strengths_at_work: She knows her assigned routes, notices when supplies are running low, and is steady about completing tasks before clocking out. She is careful not to discuss patient information in public areas. When a new procedure is explained clearly and demonstrated, she usually learns it reliably.
occupation.workplace_challenges: The job requires long periods on her feet, pushing a cart, bending, and working around changing priorities. Her back and knees can ache near the end of a shift. Online training modules and lengthy written notices take her longer than they do some coworkers, and she prefers a supervisor to explain a change directly rather than simply sending a link.
occupation.work_attitude: She takes pride in doing useful work that patients and staff may not notice unless it is done poorly. She wants fair pay and safe staffing, but is wary of managers who use cheerful slogans in place of practical solutions. She is dependable without treating work as her entire identity.

interests: Caring for her senior dog, Luna, including their unhurried neighborhood routine.
Small craft and do-it-yourself projects that have a practical result, such as hemming clothing or repairing a loose household item.
Looking at simple craft ideas and saved photographs, without wanting to turn the hobby into a business.
Occasional short drives to see family or spend a few hours somewhere pleasant nearby.
A quiet visit with her daughter and grandchildren more than a large organized gathering.
Keeping her home functional and uncluttered.
Familiar music from her youth and songs she recognizes from family gatherings.
Watching a familiar television program while resting after work.
Listening to relatives tell stories about earlier family life.
Finding a useful bargain when she genuinely needs an item.
Seeing Luna greet a familiar person or settle comfortably at home.
A brief stop at a neighborhood bakery or casual restaurant when someone else suggests it.
Keeping a few family photographs in visible places.
Practical advice from someone who has actually dealt with a similar problem.
A calm afternoon with no appointment or errand that has to be rushed.
Simple seasonal decorations that can be stored without taking up much room.
Helping a relative with a small repair or organizing task when she has the energy.
A shaded local park or a scenic view during a nearby outing, without considering outdoor recreation a hobby.
Seeing her grandchildren learn a skill or become more confident.
Having enough time to finish a task carefully instead of being hurried through it.
likes: Roasted or grilled meat with a familiar side dish, especially when the seasoning is savory rather than elaborate.
Warm tortillas, rice, beans, and other foods associated with family meals, while recognizing that her own habits do not represent every Latino household.
A modest serving of cookies with coffee or as an afternoon snack.
Coffee that is strong and uncomplicated, with a little milk or sugar depending on the day.
A home that is clean, easy to maintain, and not crowded with decorations or storage boxes.
Clear prices displayed before she agrees to buy or sign up for something.
A familiar worker at a clinic, store, or workplace who remembers how she prefers information explained.
Being given a direct answer rather than an overly polished sales pitch.
Short visits that leave room for everyone to return to their own schedule.
Her daughter calling just to share a small piece of news, not only when there is a problem.
A comfortable pair of work shoes, even if they are not stylish.
A clean bed, a quiet room, and a night when her back does not wake her.
A simple item that lasts for years and can be repaired rather than replaced.
Relatives who can disagree without insulting each other.
A practical paper checklist when a process involves several steps.
A familiar Catholic service or holiday tradition when it fits her schedule.
The feeling of having a bill paid before its due date.
A nearby drive with good company, a comfortable seat, and no complicated itinerary.
A straightforward craft project she can complete in one or two sittings.
Small, sincere gestures of thanks from people who notice her effort.
dislikes: Being pressured to buy something immediately because a supposed discount will expire.
Subscription offers that are easy to start and difficult to cancel.
Long online forms with small print, unexplained abbreviations, or repeated password requirements.
People who talk over her or assume a question means she is incapable.
Unclear medical bills and unexpected charges that take repeated calls to explain.
Shopping malls as a leisure activity, particularly when crowded or noisy.
Replacing a working appliance or phone simply because a newer model exists.
Very spicy food that overwhelms the other flavors in a meal.
Food described with unfamiliar ingredients but no plain explanation of what is in it.
Being told to solve a sleep or pain problem with a quick lifestyle tip that ignores her work schedule.
Crowded social events where she has to make small talk for hours.
Unnecessary clutter and furniture that makes cleaning harder.
People who dismiss financial strain by saying everyone should simply budget better.
Being rushed through a decision she does not yet understand.
Noisy neighbors or televisions late at night.
Long hikes, strenuous outdoor recreation, or activities that aggravate her back and knees.
Complicated phone apps required for a task that could be handled with a direct conversation.
Online arguments that turn every political disagreement into a personal attack.
Wasteful packaging and products that break quickly despite being advertised as premium.
Being treated as if her age means she is unable to learn or adapt.

food_and_drink.general_pattern: She enjoys meat-centered meals and familiar preparations such as grilling, roasting, or pan-cooking. She cooks because it is useful and because familiar food can make home feel settled, not because cooking and baking are major hobbies. She likes a recognizable plate with a clear main dish and sides, snacks frequently, and often chooses cookies when they are available.
usual_choices: Grilled chicken, pork, or beef when it is affordable and easy to prepare.
Rice, beans, potatoes, tortillas, or vegetables as uncomplicated sides.
Mild salsa or seasoning that adds flavor without making the meal painfully hot.
Leftovers packed for the next workday when there is enough to make a useful portion.
Cookies or crackers as a convenient snack, especially when she is tired.
food_and_drink.limits: She is not vegetarian and does not seek out trendy diets, unusual ingredients, or elaborate restaurant experiences. She can enjoy a vegetable dish or a lighter meal, but does not organize her identity around health food.

shopping.pattern: Shopping is an errand rather than entertainment. She buys replacements when something is worn out or genuinely needed, checks prices, and is more comfortable buying a familiar item than gambling on an unfamiliar brand.
shopping.typical_channels: She usually shops in person for groceries and household necessities because she can see the item and compare shelf prices. She may use a basic website when it clearly saves time, but avoids creating accounts, installing apps, and storing payment information unless there is a compelling reason.
shopping.spending_style: She is frugal and deliberate rather than absolutely unwilling to spend. She will pay a little more for dependable work shoes or a household item she expects to keep, but resists luxury branding, impulse purchases, and recurring fees.

traits: Organized in a practical, routine-based way; she keeps appointments and work obligations in a paper calendar.
Conscientious about tasks that affect other people, particularly cleaning standards, family plans, and promises she has made.
Generally appreciative and positive, noticing a comfortable evening, a good cup of coffee, or a kind exchange without pretending that financial stress has disappeared.
Realistic and sometimes skeptical; she wants claims supported by clear explanations rather than sales language.
Protective of her independence and uncomfortable when someone assumes she cannot make her own choices.
Patient with children, older relatives, and people who are trying in good faith, but less patient with condescension or avoidable confusion.
Private about painful feelings and more likely to say she is tired or needs a little time than to give a long emotional account.
Loyal to a small circle of relatives and coworkers, while taking time to trust new people.
Resourceful about stretching money, repairing small household problems, and finding a workable alternative when the first plan fails.
Moderately stubborn once she has decided that a product or routine is not worth the trouble.
Able to laugh at everyday annoyances and use humor to ease awkwardness, though she does not use it to dismiss serious problems.
Occasionally anxious about medical costs, retirement, and unexpected repairs, but usually responds by making a list or calling someone rather than giving up.

big_five.openness: Low to moderate. She enjoys familiar music, foods, and routines and does not seek novelty for its own sake. She can be receptive to a practical idea when it is explained plainly and she can see how it would improve daily life.
big_five.conscientiousness: High. She prefers planning, preparation, reliable routines, and completing commitments. Her organization is grounded in work habits, lists, and familiar systems rather than elaborate productivity tools.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. She can be friendly and conversational in familiar settings, but does not identify socializing as a hobby and needs quiet time after a demanding shift.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate to high. She is considerate and cooperative with people who treat her fairly, but can be firm and distrustful when she senses pressure, disrespect, or a misleading promise.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. Financial uncertainty, pain, and disrupted sleep sometimes make her worry or become irritable, but she is not constantly distressed and can still take pleasure in ordinary routines.

personality.emotional_patterns: Her first response to a problem is often to handle the concrete part: make the call, check the bill, or write down what needs doing. She may postpone talking about disappointment until she has had time to think. She can feel embarrassed when she struggles with a complex form, and responds best to patient, matter-of-fact help rather than reassurance that sounds patronizing.

beliefs: A person's freedom to make ordinary personal choices matters, and government should not intrude without a clear reason.
Being Republican describes her political affiliation, but she does not assume that every Republican position fits her.
Free expression should be protected, including speech she dislikes, though people remain responsible for how they treat others.
Government programs should be understandable and should not make it needlessly difficult for eligible people to receive help.
Progressive taxation is reasonable when it helps pay for public services and worker and family protections that reduce severe inequality.
A worker who shows up and does physically demanding work should be able to cover basic needs without being treated as disposable.
People should have a fair chance to improve their circumstances, but personal decisions and individual responsibility still matter.
She wants the federal budget deficit taken seriously because debt and poorly managed spending can create costs for people who have little room to absorb them.
Inflation is a very big problem because small price increases accumulate into real choices about food, bills, and repairs.
She rates the economy as poor, even though she does not believe every household is experiencing the same hardship.
Her own family's finances are better than they were four years ago because employment became steadier and some old expenses were reduced.
Inflation still causes moderate hardship; she can generally manage, but has to watch what she spends and delay some purchases.
Healthcare affordability is a very big problem, especially when insurance, prescriptions, and unexpected bills are difficult to predict.

She does not believe government should provide healthcare as a general responsibility for everyone in every circumstance, but supports some public programs and practical assistance for people who need it.
A healthcare system should not leave working people unable to obtain basic care because they are just above an eligibility threshold.
Drug addiction is a very big problem and should be addressed with treatment and accountability rather than pretending that it only affects other communities.
She does not rate gun violence as a very big problem, though she does not think shootings or unsafe behavior should be ignored.
She supports closing the gun-show loophole because a background-check rule should not become meaningless depending on where a firearm is sold.
She supports red-flag laws when there is a serious, evidence-based threat and there are clear protections against arbitrary use.
She supports more mental-health funding as one way of addressing gun violence and broader community distress.
She values lawful gun ownership but does not regard every proposed safety measure as an attack on that right.
Abortion should be legal in most cases; her Catholic faith may make the issue morally complicated for her, but she does not believe the law should remove every woman's choice.
Some undocumented immigrants should have a path to legal status if they meet fair requirements and are willing to follow the process.
Immigration rules should be enforced in an orderly way, but families should not be discussed as if they are a faceless threat.
Partisan unwillingness to cooperate is a very big problem because ordinary people still need roads, schools, hospitals, and functioning public services.
She is somewhat confident that elections are fair, while recognizing that administrative errors can happen and should be investigated transparently.
She does not describe democracy as very threatened, but worries that political hostility could make people distrust one another or accept violence.
She is concerned about post-election violence and believes losing an election is not a justification for intimidation or assault.
She approves of the Supreme Court, though approval does not mean she agrees with every decision it makes.
The Supreme Court and other institutions should explain their reasoning in a way the public can follow, not rely on people to take a conclusion on faith.
A Republican identity and support for some worker protections are not contradictions to her; she sees fairness and responsibility as compatible.
Public services are worthwhile when they work reliably, are funded honestly, and do not bury people in confusing rules.
People should be able to keep personal religious beliefs without using them to demean neighbors with different beliefs.
Family loyalty matters, but relatives should be allowed to make different choices and maintain their own households.
A good product should solve a real problem, last a reasonable time, and not require unnecessary fees or complicated setup.
New technology is not automatically better; a familiar tool that works reliably may be the wiser choice.
Health deserves attention, but she dislikes moralizing about food, pain, or exercise without understanding a person's circumstances.
Respect is shown in ordinary behavior, such as listening, keeping a promise, and explaining a confusing process without shaming someone.
It is possible to be grateful for improvement and still say that prices, healthcare, and work conditions remain difficult.
A peaceful disagreement is preferable to pretending that everyone in a family or community shares the same politics.
skills: Reliable hospital cleaning and room-resetting practices learned through repeated on-the-job experience.
Practical familiarity with safe handling of common cleaning products and following posted workplace procedures.
Good spatial memory for her assigned work route, supply locations, and the sequence of tasks that keeps her shift moving.
Noticing practical problems such as a spill, a missing supply, a loose fixture, or a blocked walkway and reporting them.
Budgeting ordinary expenses with a calendar, envelopes, or a basic written list, even if she has limited savings.
Comparing prices and spotting when a promotion depends on buying more than she needs.
Basic sewing and mending, including simple hems, buttons, and small fabric repairs.
Simple household troubleshooting and small do-it-yourself repairs when instructions are clear.
Conversational English and Spanish in familiar social settings, without claiming professional interpreting ability.
Learning a physical task by observing a demonstration and repeating it.
Maintaining courteous communication with patients, visitors, nurses, and coworkers while respecting privacy.
Remembering family birthdays and practical details that relatives have shared.
Using a basic smartphone for calls, texts, maps when needed, and essential work communication.
Asking a clarifying question when she recognizes that she has not understood an instruction.
Staying calm enough to complete a routine task when the hospital environment is busy or emotionally tense.

relationships.name: Elena Navarro
relationships.description: Elena lives in the Albuquerque area with her own household and has two school-age children. Teresa enjoys seeing the grandchildren and helps with occasional practical needs, but tries not to assume she is automatically available for childcare. They are affectionate and close, though Teresa can worry that her advice sounds more critical than she intends.

relationships.name: Mateo Navarro
relationships.description: Mateo lives outside Albuquerque, in Arizona, and keeps in touch by phone and text. He is more comfortable with online services than Teresa is, so she sometimes asks him to help interpret an account screen or compare a device, while making clear that the final decision is hers.

relationships.name: Arturo Navarro
relationships.description: The marriage ended several years ago. They can communicate about family matters without open hostility, but they do not share finances or rely on one another as a daily support system. Teresa prefers clear boundaries and does not romanticize the relationship.

relationships.name: Rosa Navarro
relationships.description: Rosa lives nearby and remains an important source of family connection. Teresa visits when she can and occasionally helps with an errand, but Rosa still has her own routines and is not assumed to be wholly dependent on Teresa.

relationships.name: Luna
relationships.description: Luna is a small older dog who lives with Teresa. Caring for her gives the day a dependable rhythm and provides companionship at home. Teresa plans around Luna's needs but keeps the dog's expenses in mind because her budget is limited.

relationships.name: Maribel
relationships.description: Maribel works in the same hospital department. They share practical observations about schedules and workplace changes and sometimes have coffee after a shift. Teresa values her straightforwardness and does not expect the friendship to require constant contact.

relationships.name: Daniel Ruiz
relationships.description: Daniel assigns work and handles procedural updates. Teresa respects him when he gives clear instructions and treats staff consistently; she will ask him to clarify an expectation rather than silently improvising when a new rule is involved.

occupation.title: Part-time grocery store clerk
occupation.organization: A locally owned neighborhood grocery store in Atlanta
occupation.description: Colton works approximately 12 to 16 hours in a typical week, with somewhat more hours during school breaks when his manager can offer them. He bags groceries, returns misplaced items, helps customers find ordinary products, faces shelves, and occasionally covers a register after completing the store's training. He is punctual and follows closing or opening checklists carefully, though he is not yet entrusted with cash-office duties or supervising other workers. His hourly earnings are modest and contribute to the household budget; he keeps a portion for transit, phone costs, and personal spending. He likes having clear tasks and being able to see when a shift is finished, but he dislikes last-minute schedule changes and customers who treat a young worker as if he has no say in how he is spoken to. His manager knows he is 17 and schedules him around his class and applicable youth-employment rules.

interests: Video games, especially games that reward practice, exploration, or solving a problem rather than requiring him to spend money to keep up.
Travel as an aspiration and an interest: he watches route videos and looks at maps, even though he has taken few trips that were not family visits.
Learning practical computer skills when a lesson gives him a task he can try himself.
Quiet time after a busy shift, usually with a game, a video, or music playing in the background.
A small number of online conversations with familiar friends, which feel easier to leave and rejoin than a large social gathering.
likes: Games he can play in short sessions without feeling that every evening has to become a competition.
Rocket League, Minecraft, and older or free-to-play titles that run on equipment his family already owns.
A game that lets him learn a map or mechanic through repetition instead of relying entirely on quick reflexes.
Used electronics and accessories that are in good condition and have a clear return option.
A phone case with a simple grip and no conspicuous branding.
Clear schedules posted early enough to plan around them.
A teacher or supervisor who explains the reason for a rule instead of treating questions as disrespect.
Being able to check a price online before going to a store.
Pickup options that let his mother combine errands and avoid paying delivery fees.
Plain oatmeal, rice, beans, pasta, potatoes, and other inexpensive foods that can be made into several meals.
Vegetarian chili, bean burritos, lentil soup, and familiar meals that do not require specialty ingredients.
Eggs, yogurt, cheese, and peanut butter as easy sources of protein that fit his diet.
Seasoned food with some heat, as long as the spice does not overwhelm the rest of the meal.
Frozen vegetables when fresh produce is expensive or likely to spoil before the household uses it.
Organic apples, milk, or packaged staples when the price difference is small or a discount brings them within reach.
Local peaches, greens, or other produce when a nearby market has them at a price that makes sense.
Walking for transportation or to clear his head, especially on routes where he feels safe and knows the area.
Short strength or mobility workouts that can be done indoors without equipment or a paid membership.
Travel videos that show ordinary details like bus routes, food prices, and how long a trip takes, not only luxury attractions.
A quiet corner at home where he can complete coursework without being expected to join every conversation.
dislikes: A product page that hides shipping, subscription, or service charges until the last screen.
Ads that use urgent countdowns or imply that a person is foolish if they do not buy immediately.
Unverified claims that a device is 'revolutionary' without explaining what it does better.
Being asked to buy something for the household before anyone has checked whether the money is available.
Paying more for a logo when a cheaper item appears to do the same job.
Wasteful packaging, especially when the item itself is small and the box is oversized.
Food that is marketed as healthy but is very expensive, heavily processed, or not filling.
People treating vegetarianism as a challenge, a joke, or an invitation to test whether he will eat meat.
Having a meal choice made for him without checking whether it fits his diet.
Overcooked vegetables and meals made needlessly bland in the name of being healthy.
A crowded shopping center when he has already spent the day around customers.
Unnecessary group activities where participation is treated as proof of being friendly.
Long phone calls about simple matters when a clear text would do.
Late schedule changes that leave him scrambling to rearrange work, class, and transportation.
Adults who interpret a cautious question as defiance before hearing what he is asking.
People who make confident financial advice sound easy while ignoring rent, wages, or family obligations.
Notifications that keep appearing after he has decided to stop using an app for the night.
Spoilers for a game or show he has not finished.
Being rushed to answer a serious question in front of other people.
Having his quietness described as laziness, rudeness, or a lack of gratitude.
preferences.culinary_profile: Vegetarian by personal choice, principally because he dislikes the idea of animals being killed for food and because the diet feels consistent with his own values. He eats dairy and eggs and does not insist that the rest of his family eat the same way. He prefers filling, familiar meals over elaborate food, is open to moderate spice, and sees food as both pleasure and a practical budget decision. He wants organic or local ingredients when they are affordable, not at the cost of leaving the household short on essentials.
preferences.shopping_profile: He prefers online comparison and ordering when it saves time or makes it easier to check specifications, reviews, and return rules. He is still a minor and does not independently make large purchases; for many orders he uses a family account or asks his mother first. He is price-conscious, checks total cost including delivery, and may abandon a purchase after a second look if it is not necessary. For groceries, he is comfortable with a mix of online price checking, store pickup, and in-person shopping.
preferences.health_consciousness_profile: He tries to eat minimally processed or organic food when the price and access make it realistic, but he is not rigid about labels and often buys conventional staples. He values movement and tries to stay active, though his routine is shaped by school, work, transit, and available space. His health choices are mostly practical rather than driven by wellness trends.
preferences.new_product_profile: Cautious but not reflexively opposed. He looks for independent reviews, clear specifications, safety information, privacy settings, durability, and a return policy. He is more willing to try a new low-cost app or game than an expensive device, a recurring subscription, or a product that collects personal information.
preferences.cultural_profile: His own family background is White and non-Hispanic, while his Atlanta school, workplace, and neighborhood bring him into regular contact with people from different racial, religious, and regional communities. He adjusts how formal he is and what references he uses across home, work, church, and class without treating that everyday flexibility as a performance.

traits: Organized in ways that help him feel less at the mercy of last-minute demands; he keeps school deadlines, work shifts, and family errands in a phone calendar.
Conscientious about commitments he has agreed to, particularly showing up for work and not leaving his mother to wonder where he is.
Guarded and skeptical of broad promises, influencer recommendations, and sales pitches, but willing to revise his view when someone gives him specific evidence.
Practical rather than status-driven; he pays attention to whether something works, lasts, and fits the actual budget.
Quietly caring toward his younger sister, though he sometimes expresses care by fixing a problem or making sure she has what she needs rather than talking about feelings.
Private about embarrassment and uncertainty; he may say he is 'fine' before he is ready to explain what is bothering him.
Persistent when a task has clear steps, but prone to stalling when a choice is vague and seems to have expensive consequences.
Fairly patient with routine and repetition, especially when he can see a reason for the procedure.
Independent-minded about food and purchases; he does not want relatives or friends to turn his vegetarian diet into a debate or a personality label.
Socially selective rather than hostile; he enjoys a few familiar people and can be courteous in a group without wanting to stay for hours.
More hopeful about concrete near-term improvements than grand predictions about how his entire life will turn out.
Sensitive to being underestimated because of his age, and more likely to become clipped or stubborn when an adult dismisses a reasonable question.
Capable of admitting a mistake after he has cooled down, although his first response may be to explain why he made the choice.
Curious about how devices, games, and practical systems work, but not interested in every new trend just because it is new.
Can be overly self-reliant about small problems and wait too long before asking for help, partly because he does not want to add another task to his mother's day.

big_five.openness: Moderate. He is interested in unfamiliar places, games, and practical technologies, and he is willing to try a new food when he understands what is in it. He is not drawn to novelty for its own sake and wants a clear reason before changing a routine or trusting a product.
big_five.conscientiousness: High for his age. He uses reminders, keeps track of shifts and course deadlines, and takes obligations seriously. His organization is a tool for managing a crowded schedule rather than evidence that he is perfectly disciplined; late-night phone use and uncertain assignments can still throw him off.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. He is not socially anxious in every setting, but extended groups and unplanned conversation tire him. He is more talkative with two or three trusted people, during a game, or when discussing a concrete problem.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate to high. He is considerate, generally cooperative, and reluctant to create trouble for coworkers or family. He is not automatically compliant: he questions unfair instructions, dislikes being pressured, and can be blunt when he thinks someone is making an unsupported claim.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. Money uncertainty, changes to plans, and fear of letting family down can make him tense and lead to rumination. He usually contains that worry in public, and he can settle himself by making a list, checking the facts, or talking to a trusted person.

beliefs: A promise is only useful if the person making it can explain what they will actually do and when.
Being skeptical is not the same as assuming everyone is lying; it is a way to avoid agreeing before he understands the details.
A person's age should not be treated as proof that their questions or observations do not matter.
Adults can have experience and still be mistaken, so listening respectfully does not require agreeing automatically.
It is better to admit that he does not know something than to pretend expertise and create a bigger problem later.
A reliable routine can make a difficult week more manageable, even when it cannot fix the underlying financial pressure.
Keeping a commitment matters, but a person should be able to explain when circumstances make a commitment impossible.
Money problems are not always caused by careless spending; rent, wages, health costs, and irregular hours can leave little room to maneuver.
A purchase is not a good deal if the household cannot afford it or if it creates a recurring charge that nobody noticed.
Saving a little money is worthwhile, but he does not believe that every inexpensive option is automatically safe or durable.
People deserve meals that fit their values and dietary needs without having to defend those needs at every table.
His vegetarian choice is personal and he does not expect family members to adopt it, but he expects them to respect it.
Organic labels can be meaningful to some people, but he does not think a family is irresponsible for buying conventional food when it costs less.
Food that is filling, safe, and affordable is more useful to his household than a perfect-looking diet that is impossible to maintain.
Exercise helps his mood and energy, but he does not think someone should be shamed for being inactive when they face health or access barriers.
Privacy matters even when a person has nothing to hide, because personal data can be used in ways the user did not agree to.
A product company should explain what information its app collects and make basic privacy choices understandable.
Online reviews can reveal real problems, but he knows that reviews may be sponsored, exaggerated, or based on a different person's needs.
New technology is useful when it solves a real problem; novelty by itself is not a good reason to spend money.
A return policy is part of the real price of trying something new, especially when a household cannot absorb a wasted purchase.
Family members should help one another, but a teenager should not be expected to become a substitute parent or solve adult financial problems alone.
He wants to be useful at home without pretending that his part-time wages can carry the full household.
Being kind to a customer or coworker is worthwhile, but kindness should not mean accepting disrespect without any boundary.
Church can give people community, continuity, and a place to ask moral questions, even when individual members practice at different levels.
He believes faith can be sincere without a person having an immediate answer to every difficult question.
A person's religious identity does not tell him everything about their politics, character, or private life.
Travel can make a place feel less abstract, but online maps and videos are not a substitute for learning how people actually live there.
Public transit and nearby services can create opportunity, but a route that exists on a map is not necessarily convenient or reliable in real life.
Doing a job well matters, but work should not consume every part of a person's life simply because the worker is young.
He believes people should be judged more by their consistent actions than by polished statements about their values.
He is not yet settled on most public-policy questions and does not want a family member, social-media post, or campaign to tell him which view a 'good person' must hold.
At 17, he understands that he is still learning about elections, government, and policy; he may ask questions or express concerns without claiming a finished political position.
People can disagree about difficult issues and still owe one another honesty, basic respect, and a willingness to distinguish facts from rumors.
skills: Keeps a usable calendar of work shifts, course deadlines, and family commitments, and checks it before agreeing to new plans.
Can follow a multistep checklist reliably, especially for store tasks and straightforward technical troubleshooting.
Has basic computer literacy and can install ordinary software, adjust common settings, and search for a specific error message.
Is learning how to diagnose simple computer and device problems by checking connections, restarting equipment, and narrowing down likely causes.
Can compare online prices and product specifications without treating the highest-rated item as automatically best.
Reads everyday instructions, labels, work notices, and class material adequately, though dense or unfamiliar technical writing takes him longer.
Can communicate politely with customers and ask a coworker for help when a request is outside his training.
Knows several budget vegetarian meals and can prepare simple food safely, though cooking is a necessity rather than a hobby.
Can navigate familiar Atlanta bus routes and plan extra time for transfers, while recognizing that transit options are uneven across the metro area.
Maintains basic personal and device privacy settings and is careful about sharing passwords or financial information.
Can stick with repetitive practice in games or coursework when progress is visible.
Is physically capable of walking regularly and doing basic indoor exercise without special equipment.

relationships.name: Denise Hayes
relationships.description: Denise works variable part-time hours as a home-care aide. She is responsible for rent, major household decisions, and arranging most of the family's appointments. Colton respects how much she manages but sometimes avoids telling her about a worry until he has a possible solution, because he does not want to add to her stress. Their relationship is affectionate but ordinary: they can be impatient with each other about chores, phone use, and scheduling, then settle back into cooperation.

relationships.name: Maya Hayes
relationships.description: Maya lives with Colton and their mother. She is in middle school and sometimes asks him for help with a device, a game, or a school problem. He cares about her and keeps an eye on her when his mother is delayed, but he is not her parent and can become annoyed when she interrupts his coursework or borrows something without asking.

relationships.name: Frankie Hayes
relationships.description: Frankie lives in the Atlanta area and is a steady connection to the family's church and extended relatives. She sometimes invites Colton to Sunday service or a family meal and is more openly religious than he is. He values her reliability and stories, while occasionally feeling that she assumes he shares every opinion she does.

relationships.name: Marcus Bell
relationships.relationship: Friend from school and online gaming
relationships.description: Marcus is one of the people Colton is comfortable messaging without needing to make a formal plan. They play games and trade occasional jokes or practical advice. They do not talk seriously every day, and gaps in conversation do not usually mean that either one is angry.

relationships.name: Tiana Brooks
relationships.description: Tiana is more talkative and socially outgoing than Colton, and sometimes invites him to inexpensive food spots or events. He appreciates that she asks rather than assuming he will attend. He may decline if the cost or transportation is unclear, but he does not take her invitations for granted.

relationships.name: Mr. Alvarez
relationships.description: Mr. Alvarez posts the schedule, trains Colton on store procedures, and expects him to ask before improvising with a customer issue. Colton finds him direct and generally fair. He is comfortable requesting clarification from him, though he dislikes being asked to cover a shift at the last minute.

relationships.name: Ms. Price
relationships.description: Ms. Price teaches Colton's introductory computer-support course. Her practical demonstrations make the material easier for him to follow. He is more likely to ask her a focused question after class than to speak up in front of the entire room.

relationships.name: Evan Hayes
relationships.description: Evan is not part of Colton's household. They have occasional contact, and his support and availability are not fully dependable. Colton's feelings about this are mixed: he would like more consistency but tries not to build plans around promises that have not been confirmed.

occupation.title: Application Support Analyst
occupation.organization: A regional hospital network based in the Philadelphia area
occupation.employment_status: Employed full-time and participating in the labor force.
occupation.annual_pay: Approximately $78,400 in base pay, with occasional small overtime or on-call payments. This is his household's sole regular income.
occupation.description: Darius supports the software used by hospital and clinic staff for scheduling, internal records, and routine administrative workflows. He responds to service tickets, reproduces reported problems, checks access permissions, reviews system logs, documents fixes, and escalates issues that require a software vendor or senior engineer. He sometimes uses SQL queries and spreadsheets to verify whether a problem affects one user or a wider group. He is not a clinician and does not make medical decisions; his contribution is keeping familiar business systems usable and explaining technical problems in practical terms.
occupation.work_style: He is strongest when a problem can be reproduced and tested step by step. He writes concise ticket notes, follows change-control procedures, and tries to avoid making an unverified fix during a busy clinic shift. When internal documentation is needlessly dense, he makes his own checklist or asks a colleague to confirm an interpretation rather than pretending he understood.
occupation.workplace_strengths: Users appreciate that he does not make them feel foolish for asking for help. He can translate between a frustrated staff member's account of what happened and the technical details needed by an engineering team. His weaknesses are that he can spend too long polishing notes, has little patience for vague requests marked urgent without context, and sometimes puts off asking for clarification when a more senior person sounds impatient.
occupation.career_path: He started with entry-level desktop and account support after community college, learned the hospital's systems over several years, and moved into application support. His experience is practical and organization-specific; he does not present himself as a software architect, data scientist, or cybersecurity expert.

Following local Philadelphia news when it directly affects neighborhoods, transportation, schools, or public services.

Occasional meals with his mother, sister, or a close friend, rather than frequent group outings.
Learning a new workplace tool when there is a clear use for it.

culinary_detail.overall_pattern: He is an omnivore who relies frequently on prepared meals, takeout, grocery deli items, and simple reheating. He does not regard cooking or baking as a hobby, though he can assemble uncomplicated meals when convenient.
regular_choices: Rotisserie chicken with a prepared side when he wants a familiar meal without cooking.
Rice bowls or a chicken sandwich ordered from a nearby takeout place.
Deli sandwiches, soup, or prepared meals on nights when work has run late.
Fruit, yogurt, or a snack bar for a quick breakfast rather than a cooked meal.
Packaged snacks kept in a desk drawer for busy workdays.
A takeout dinner with relatives when someone else has chosen the restaurant.
A prepared salad or vegetables when he can get them without paying a large convenience premium.
culinary_detail.taste_and_constraints: He likes familiar flavors, moderate seasoning, and food that is satisfying without being elaborate. He will choose minimally processed, organic, or locally sourced options when the price and availability make sense, but he does not treat those labels as absolute rules. Limited time, energy, confidence, and interest in cooking all affect what he actually eats.

shopping_detail.pattern: He shops for groceries and essentials when needed, but treats nonessential shopping as occasional entertainment. He compares prices online, checks promotional offers, and sometimes buys something on impulse when a sale or appealing display catches his attention.
shopping_detail.spending_boundary: He usually gives himself a rough personal limit for a shopping trip and tries to avoid purchases that would interfere with rent, savings, or a planned bill. His limit is not infallible: a good-looking household item or a useful piece of tech can tempt him, especially after a stressful week.
shopping_detail.channels: He uses online ordering for familiar items, returns when delivery is unreliable, and prefers to inspect clothing or home goods in person when fit and finish matter. He does not insist on one shopping channel.

preferences.cultural_and_media_tastes: He is shaped by Philadelphia and Black American family life, but also by global streaming, music, online communities, and stories from multiple countries. He is interested in contemporary culture without wanting every part of his life to be trend-driven. He enjoys learning about other places from media more than arranging frequent international travel.

traits: Thoughtful: he tends to consider what a person meant, not only the exact words they used, and can replay a conversation later to see whether he missed something.
Reserved: he is comfortable being around people but prefers a few genuine connections to a large, constantly active social circle.
Welcoming: he will greet a new coworker, explain a routine, or make a visitor feel less lost without needing to become their close friend.
Cautious about trust: he pays attention to whether people keep small promises before relying on them with something important.
Practical: when a problem feels overwhelming, he looks for the next step he can actually take rather than making a grand plan.
Quietly curious: he enjoys learning about unfamiliar places, music, and ideas through reading and online media, especially when they are explained clearly.
Self-respecting: he does not like being talked down to, particularly about his reading difficulty or education, and becomes firm if someone mistakes patience for passivity.
Moderately disciplined: he can maintain recurring work, health, and bill-paying routines, though he still has to manage screen distraction and occasional impulse purchases.
Dryly humorous: he uses understated jokes to ease tension and is more likely to tease himself than to perform for a whole room.
Fair-minded but skeptical: he wants rules applied consistently, while remaining alert to the possibility that official explanations leave out inconvenient facts.
Loyal to family: he responds when close relatives need help, but is learning not to say yes automatically when the request is beyond his time or budget.
Conflict-avoidant at first: he often gives a minor annoyance a chance to resolve itself, then becomes quite direct when it repeatedly affects his work or boundaries.
Emotionally steady in a crisis: he can focus on a checklist during a technical outage or family emergency, then feel the stress later when things have quieted down.
Sensitive to humiliation: correction is acceptable when it is specific and respectful; public embarrassment or condescension can stay with him for days.
Independent-minded: he prefers to form his own view and dislikes being treated as if a political party, church, employer, or online group should decide what he thinks.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. He is interested in global media, contemporary culture, and unfamiliar ideas, and he enjoys small creative projects; he is less enthusiastic about novelty that feels expensive, chaotic, or poorly explained.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderately high. He keeps dependable work and preventive-health routines, documents technical tasks, and tries to stay within a budget, but can procrastinate on complex paperwork and loses track of time online.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. He is thoughtful and reserved, recovers through quiet time, and does not seek socializing as a hobby. He can nevertheless be sociable, welcoming, and articulate in a familiar one-to-one setting.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high with boundaries. He is courteous, helpful, and considerate, but does not equate being agreeable with accepting unfair treatment or pretending to trust someone.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. He is not chronically volatile, but uncertainty about money, healthcare, job changes, and political trust can make him ruminate. He generally functions through worry by checking facts, making a list, or talking to one trusted person.

beliefs: Darius identifies primarily as an Independent and is uncomfortable treating party membership as a complete account of a person's judgment.
He leans libertarian in the sense that he values personal liberty, private choice, free expression, and limits on unnecessary government control.
He believes individuals should generally be able to make personal decisions about their relationships, private lives, and lawful conduct without intrusive state interference.
He believes competitive markets and private enterprise usually generate useful services and prosperity when people can make informed choices.
He also believes market competition does not excuse fraud, monopoly behavior, unsafe practices, or deliberate concealment of fees.
He is wary of government programs that lack a clear purpose, transparent cost, or accountability for results.
He believes government should provide a meaningful healthcare option or baseline because medical needs are unavoidable and market pricing can leave people exposed.
He sees no contradiction between a restrained government and a basic healthcare guarantee, provided the arrangement is understandable, sustainable, and not needlessly wasteful.
He considers healthcare affordability a very big public problem, partly because insured people can still face confusing bills and large out-of-pocket costs.
He considers inflation a very big problem and experiences moderate hardship from higher everyday prices, even though he can generally pay his bills.
He considers drug addiction a very big problem and believes treatment and mental-health support matter alongside public safety.
He considers the federal budget deficit a very big problem and wants elected officials to explain how new commitments will be paid for.
He considers gun violence a very big public problem, particularly when ordinary people and communities bear the consequences of poor safeguards.
He supports closing the gun-show loophole because he thinks similar transactions should be governed by consistent rules.
He supports red-flag laws when they include due process, clear standards, and a real opportunity for a person to challenge an order.
He supports increased mental-health funding as part of gun-violence prevention, while doubting that any single intervention can solve the problem alone.
He considers the lack of cooperation between political parties a very big problem because it makes practical public services harder to maintain.
He supports abortion being legal in all cases, even though his Protestant background can make some parts of the issue emotionally serious rather than abstract.
He does not believe his personal religious views should automatically become criminal rules for everyone else.
He supports deportation as a policy response in cases where immigration law has been violated, especially for people with serious criminal convictions or a final order after due process.

His support for deportation does not mean he opposes every legal route to status; he can support a defined legal process for some long-settled people while wanting enforcement rules to mean something.
He considers the economy not so good: he can acknowledge that his own household finances have improved while noticing that essentials remain expensive and many people are worse off.
He reports that his family's financial situation is better than it was four years earlier, largely because his employment became steadier and his income rose.

He is not at all confident that elections are fair. His doubt is shaped by partisan administration, inconsistent claims, and distrust of institutions; he does not claim to possess proof that a particular result was fraudulent.
He is concerned about post-election violence and thinks losing political groups should not treat threats or intimidation as normal civic behavior.

He does not describe democracy as very threatened in the broadest sense; he thinks its institutions are strained but still functioning, which is distinct from his lack of confidence in election fairness.

He disapproves of the Supreme Court, particularly when he perceives decisions as overly partisan or detached from ordinary consequences, but does not think disagreement makes the Court's existence illegitimate.
He believes that public policy should be judged by what it does to people's daily lives, not merely by whether its supporters use the correct political language.
He prefers rules that are clear and applied consistently, and becomes suspicious when powerful people seem to receive exceptions unavailable to ordinary residents.
He thinks a job should provide fair pay and predictable expectations, but he does not believe that a person's occupation determines their worth.
He views reading difficulty as a practical access issue, not a measure of intelligence, and believes instructions and public services should be understandable to the people expected to use them.
His Protestant faith gives him a language for gratitude, accountability, and forgiveness, but his observance varies and he does not claim that every Christian shares his political views.

He thinks people should be able to disagree without immediately treating one another as enemies, although he recognizes that some disagreements involve real harms rather than mere differences of taste.
He values privacy and consent in personal life, including the freedom to decline a social invitation or withhold personal information.
He believes health is influenced by individual choices, access to care, work schedules, money, and the neighborhood environment, rather than by willpower alone.
He thinks a good product should be honest about its price, limitations, and instructions, and does not regard novelty by itself as an improvement.
He believes family support is important but should not require one person to carry every practical or financial burden without discussion.
He thinks local community services can matter more to a household than distant political arguments, even though he follows national issues.
He believes that public safety and civil liberties both matter, and that authorities should explain the limits and safeguards of powers they ask people to accept.

relationships.name: Denise Coleman
relationships.description: Denise lives in Philadelphia and is one of Darius's most trusted people. They exchange texts several times a week and sometimes share a meal or run an errand together. He respects her judgment but is trying to distinguish support from automatically taking responsibility for every problem.

relationships.name: Nia Coleman
relationships.description: Nia works in a different field and is more socially outgoing than Darius. They share family updates, send each other links and jokes, and occasionally disagree about politics without treating the disagreement as a reason to end the relationship.

relationships.name: Marcus Reed
relationships.description: Marcus is a longtime friend from Darius's earlier working years. They are comfortable spending time together without a large plan, and Marcus is one of the people Darius might ask for an honest opinion about a purchase, job move, or family dilemma.

relationships.name: Tasha Green
relationships.description: Tasha and Darius occasionally exchange messages about work, reading, and local places to eat. They are friendly and supportive but do not need to speak every week to consider the friendship intact.

relationships.name: Leon Brooks
relationships.description: Leon has more experience with the hospital's internal systems and is a useful source of technical perspective. Darius values his calm explanations, while sometimes feeling reluctant to ask Leon questions when the office is busy.

relationships.name: Priya Shah
relationships.description: Priya works on related systems and is good at turning unclear tickets into concrete tests. Darius trusts her work and exchanges concise handoffs with her; they are friendly without turning the workplace relationship into an obligation to socialize outside work.

relationships.name: Reverend James Carter
relationships.relationship: Pastor at a Protestant congregation he attends intermittently
relationships.description: Darius appreciates Reverend Carter's measured approach and practical concern for people in the neighborhood. Darius is not present every Sunday, but attends some services and family occasions and keeps a respectful connection.

relationships.name: Dating relationships
relationships.relationship: Occasional dating, not currently a committed partnership
relationships.description: Darius has never been married and is not currently in a serious relationship. He is open to dating when it feels mutual and unforced, but he is cautious about oversharing, rushing commitment, or treating a relationship as proof that he has reached a particular stage of adulthood.

Gabriel Leon Sandoval.nationality: American; a U.S. citizen by birth

occupation.current_status: Not employed; outside the labor force and not actively looking for a job.
occupation.current_role: His main day-to-day responsibilities are managing his health, keeping up with household administration, and parenting his 14-year-old son. He does not describe caregiving as a career, and he is not currently doing paid work.
occupation.previous_work: Previously worked as a shipping-and-receiving and inventory clerk at a regional distribution warehouse. He scanned incoming goods, checked packing slips, organized pallets, recorded discrepancies, prepared outgoing orders, and coordinated with drivers and floor supervisors. Earlier in that job he worked rotating shifts, which left him accustomed to odd hours.
occupation.reason_for_leaving_work: A back injury sustained at work in 2019 developed into persistent lower-back pain and intermittent sciatica. After attempts at modified duties and rehabilitation, he stopped working and eventually received disability benefits. He is wary of work that could aggravate the injury or jeopardize benefits before he knows whether he can sustain it.
occupation.skills_and_working_style: He was dependable with concrete procedures, inventory counts, and catching mismatches between a label and a shipment. He was not a supervisor or a logistics executive; his expertise came from repeated hands-on work, a certificate, and learning how the warehouse actually functioned.
occupation.organization: No current employer.

interests: Keeping up with local Las Vegas news, weather, traffic, and community issues through phone feeds.
Watching short explainers and commentary videos when a topic catches his attention.
Listening to sports talk and familiar radio stations while doing household tasks, without treating sports as a serious hobby.
Following discussions about national politics, elections, public safety, and the cost of healthcare.

Finding practical answers online about benefits, school forms, repairs, and medical appointments.

likes: Mild, straightforward meals with familiar ingredients and no surprising heat.

A little lime or mild salsa on the side, so he can control how much flavor he adds.
A familiar Mexican American family dish when a relative prepares it, provided it is not very spicy.
Food served at a comfortable temperature and not crowded together in complicated combinations.
A quiet booth or uncrowded table where he can talk with his son without shouting.
Businesses where staff answer direct questions plainly and do not make him feel rushed.
A sturdy, familiar brand of shoes that he already knows will not aggravate his back.
A phone with a simple interface, reliable battery, and a recognizable warranty.
Being able to return an item in person if it does not work as expected.
A clean, cool room after walking in desert heat.
A predictable route through familiar streets and shops.
An unhurried conversation with someone who can disagree without insulting him.
Short videos that explain a complicated issue in plain language.
Old family photos and stories, even if he does not always know the names of every person in them.
A familiar comedy that does not demand much attention after a long day.
A regular, gentle walk that leaves him feeling looser rather than exhausted.
A clean pair of work-style clothes and a fresh haircut when he has an appointment.
Practical gifts for his son that are useful rather than decorative.
Having his choices respected, especially when the choice involves his health or money.
The feeling of being able to handle a necessary errand without asking someone else to do it.
Local businesses where he recognizes the layout and knows roughly what things cost.

Menus that use elaborate descriptions but do not make clear what is actually in the food.
Being pressured to try something new after he has already said no.
Companies that change an app or product interface without explaining what has changed.
Salespeople who treat a limited budget as a reason to speak down to him.
Paying a premium for a product that has no clear advantage beyond its image.
Cheap items that fail quickly and force him to spend twice, even when the better-quality option is hard to afford.
Shopping centers when they are crowded, hot, or noisy.
Long phone trees and customer-service transfers that make him repeat the same explanation.
Medical bills that arrive without an understandable breakdown.
Being told that he is lazy or simply needs to work harder when pain limits what he can sustain.
People who assume that being widowed means he should already be “over it.”
Crowded nightlife, loud bars, and events where he cannot easily sit down or leave.
Overnight travel with unfamiliar logistics and no clear way to manage a pain flare-up.
Very formal conversation that feels like a test of status or education.
Political arguments where the other person assigns him a belief he has not expressed.
Food that is greasy, unusually sweet, or made from a complicated mix of textures.
Unsolicited religious pressure, even though he respects that relatives find meaning in faith.
Promises of quick financial fixes or miracle health products.
Being asked to make several difficult decisions while tired or in pain.
A cluttered phone screen full of alerts, even though he checks social media often.
People who use personal information he shared in confidence to win an argument.
The implication that his son should carry adult responsibilities because household money is tight.
preferences.culinary_tastes: Prefers mild, simple flavors. He avoids hot spice, strong aromas, unfamiliar textures, and complicated combinations, but does not reject every new dish if he can see what it contains and choose a small portion.
preferences.shopping_habits: Shopping is a practical chore rather than a leisure activity. He compares prices on essentials, but is brand-conscious when a familiar product seems more dependable, easier to return, or more comfortable. He may pay somewhat more for a known phone, shoe, or household item when he can manage it, yet his income usually forces him to prioritize rent, food, transportation, and health costs.
preferences.health_consciousness: He tries to prioritize physical and mental well-being in ways that are realistic with chronic pain and limited money. Regular walking and attending necessary appointments matter to him; he is not rigid about food or celebrations and does not regard himself as an expert on health.
preferences.attitude_toward_new_products: Strongly resistant to changes in routine or products when he sees no clear benefit. He worries that many new offerings add cost, complexity, or hidden subscriptions. If a trusted person demonstrates an obvious practical advantage, he may reconsider after taking time to think.
preferences.cultural_influences: His father’s Mexican American family ties are important to him through relatives, family expressions, food, music, and stories. He participates in some family traditions without identifying with the Catholic faith himself, and he also lives comfortably within broader U.S. culture.
preferences.travel_habits: A homebody who finds comfort in familiar surroundings and chooses local recreation over overnight or international trips. He will make necessary trips to see family or attend an appointment, but usually wants the route and arrangements to be predictable.
preferences.lifestyle: Highly irregular. A former rotating-shift schedule, chronic pain, medical appointments, school obligations, and the disruptions of bereavement make it hard to keep a consistent sleep or leisure routine. His current housing is subsidized and comparatively stable, but he worries about renewal and unexpected expenses.

traits: Friendly on first contact, but slow to grant deep trust.
Curious about unfamiliar subjects and willing to listen when a speaker does not sound condescending.
Strongly attached to familiar routines, brands, and ways of doing necessary tasks.
Protective of his son and sensitive to anything he reads as a threat to the child’s stability.
Practical: he tends to ask what can actually be done this week before entertaining a sweeping plan.
Proud, sometimes to his own disadvantage; he dislikes being treated as helpless because he receives disability benefits.
Politically stubborn, especially when he believes someone is dismissing working people or local communities.
Capable of patience with children, customer-service staff, and people navigating a problem in good faith.
More pessimistic about institutions than about individual people he knows personally.
Grieving in an uneven, private way; ordinary reminders of his wife can affect his mood without warning.
Cautious with money, yet still drawn to familiar labels and recognizable quality when a purchase matters to him.
Occasionally defensive when his education or work history is underestimated.
Able to tolerate uncertainty in discussion, but uncomfortable with uncertainty about housing, health, or income.
Sociable in a low-key way, though he does not consider socializing a hobby.
Resourceful when a concrete household problem needs solving, less consistent with plans that require a long, uninterrupted routine.

big_five.openness: Moderately high (72/100). He enjoys exploring unfamiliar topics and can entertain competing explanations, but this openness does not make him eager to replace established products or routines.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate-low (43/100). He can be careful and dependable when a task affects his son, benefits, or bills, but pain, poor sleep, and unpredictable obligations make his routines uneven.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate (58/100). He is sociable, comfortable with casual conversation, and more animated around people he trusts, while still preferring small-scale contact to busy social events.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate-high (62/100). He is generous and courteous when treated respectfully, but his distrust of institutions and strong opinions can make him blunt or hard to persuade.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderately high (67/100). Financial uncertainty, pain, bereavement, and political conflict can keep him tense; he can also settle himself through a walk, familiar entertainment, or a practical task.

beliefs: He identifies as an Independent because he does not want either major party to claim his loyalty, even though his political outlook is strongly conservative.
He believes tradition gives families and communities continuity, but that a tradition should not be used as an excuse to mistreat people.
He places high value on religious and cultural continuity in society while remaining personally agnostic and unaffiliated with a religion.
He thinks people should be allowed to keep a private faith without being pressured to make it a test of belonging.
He believes the federal government should have substantially limited responsibilities and that local communities often understand their own needs better.
He favors lower taxes and fewer regulations, particularly when he thinks rules burden small businesses or working people without clear benefit.
He believes individuals and families generally make better day-to-day spending decisions than federal agencies.
He nevertheless thinks government can provide a limited safety net for people with severe disabilities, children, and people who cannot meet basic needs.
He does not believe government should provide healthcare as a general, universal responsibility, but supports some public programs that protect people in specific circumstances.
He considers healthcare affordability a very big problem because insurance does not always make appointments, prescriptions, dental care, or bills manageable.
He sees drug addiction as a very big problem and thinks treatment and mental-health services should be part of a serious response.
He does not rate the federal budget deficit as a very big problem compared with immediate household concerns, though he dislikes wasteful spending.
He does not rate inflation as a very big public problem. Prices matter to him, but he attributes his family’s financial decline mainly to lost earnings and bereavement rather than inflation.
He reports no inflation-related hardship in the survey sense: he has not recently skipped essentials specifically because prices rose, partly because benefits and assistance cover some basics.
He says his household’s financial situation is worse than it was four years ago because his wife died and his work income ended.

He rates the overall economy as excellent when judging national capacity and business activity, even though he is personally financially constrained; he does not equate the national economy with his household budget.
He does not rate gun violence as a very big problem in the broad public-priority sense, but he still takes individual threats and unsafe handling seriously.
He strongly supports gun rights and believes lawful ownership is an important form of personal responsibility and protection.
He supports closing the gun-show loophole because he believes background checks should not depend on the venue where a gun is sold.
He supports red-flag laws when they include due process, credible evidence, and a meaningful way for a person to challenge an order.
He supports increased mental-health funding as a gun-violence measure and thinks prevention should receive more attention than slogans about punishment alone.
He believes abortion should be illegal in most cases, while allowing that rare, serious circumstances require exceptions and should be handled with compassion.
He supports a path to legal status for at least some undocumented immigrants who have longstanding ties, especially when they have worked, raised families, and followed the law in other ways.
He also favors stronger border enforcement and national sovereignty; to him, supporting legal status for some people does not mean supporting an unregulated border.
He thinks the country is deeply polarized and views the lack of cooperation between political parties as a very big problem.
He believes democracy is very threatened, especially by escalating distrust, political intimidation, and the tendency to treat opponents as enemies.
He is not very confident that elections are fair, but his skepticism is general and institutional rather than a claim that every election result is fabricated.
He is concerned about post-election violence and thinks political leaders should lower the temperature rather than hint that violence is acceptable.
