She expects that a cup can hold a drink and that a plate is associated with food.
She has begun to understand that some actions, such as pushing a toy, make something move.
She recognizes that adults can help when a toy, zipper, or container is difficult.
She often expects a repeated game to happen in roughly the same way each time.
She can anticipate familiar parts of a routine when the first step begins.
She seems to understand simple safety warnings better when an adult points to the relevant object or place.
She recognizes familiar family members by voice, appearance, and the way they greet her.
She expects comfort from familiar adults when she is frightened or hurt.
She can tell that some foods are for eating and some play materials are not, with reminders.
She knows that a closed door or a caregiver's attention can temporarily keep her from entering or joining.
She expects that toys can be picked up and played with again later, though waiting for that later can be difficult.
She has started to understand that other children may want the same toy she wants.
She may assume that a person can see what she is pointing at, even when the person is looking elsewhere.
She learns that a word can name an object when a familiar adult repeats the word while showing it.
She understands some simple differences such as hot and cold, big and small, or wet and dry through direct experience.
She sometimes treats pretend play as if it were real while remaining able to shift back when an adult clarifies.
She is learning that a small bump or frustration does not always mean something is permanently broken.
She expects adults to set boundaries, although her acceptance of those boundaries depends on her immediate state.
She can recognize that a request to wait means not immediately, but has limited ability to estimate how long.
She is beginning to connect putting on shoes with going outside or getting into the car.
She recognizes familiar phrases in both English and Spanish without necessarily using either language in every situation.
She may expect that a caregiver will notice when she is proud of something she has made.
She is learning that simple apologies, comforting gestures, or returning a toy can help after a small conflict.
She does not yet hold a stable, abstract view of politics, religion, money, health policy, or other adult public issues.
skills: Communicates many everyday wants and needs in short phrases, gestures, and pointing.
Recognizes familiar caregivers, classmates, household objects, and repeated routines.
Can follow some simple one-step directions when she is attentive and the words are familiar.
Uses imitation effectively to learn a new play action or household routine.
Enjoys turning pages in sturdy picture books and identifying familiar images.
Can make marks with chunky crayons when given suitable materials and supervision.
Practices basic self-help tasks such as attempting to put on shoes or washing hands with adult assistance.
Can participate in simple pretend play and assign familiar roles to toys.
Uses a spoon and cup with age-appropriate spills and continued adult oversight.
Can walk, run, climb, and play in familiar spaces, while still needing close supervision near streets, water, stairs, and parking areas.
Shows early awareness of when a situation is unfamiliar and can seek a caregiver.
Is learning to take turns with adult coaching but cannot reliably do so without help.

relationships.name: Elena Alvarez
relationships.description: Elena works as a medical billing specialist at a local clinic. She handles most preschool coordination and daily routines, and tries to give Camila simple explanations before transitions. Work demands and household costs can leave her tired, but she is attentive to Camila's cues.

relationships.name: Rosa Alvarez
relationships.description: Rosa lives with Camila and Elena, helps with preschool pickups and meals, and speaks Spanish frequently at home. She is affectionate and often uses familiar songs, food, and family stories to comfort Camila, while sometimes having different ideas from Elena about how quickly a child should learn a routine.

relationships.name: Daniel
relationships.description: Daniel has regular contact with Camila, usually through planned visits coordinated with Elena. Camila recognizes him and is generally comfortable with him, though she may need a little time to settle into a handoff if she is tired or the schedule has changed.

relationships.name: Preschool teacher
relationships.description: Camila's teacher provides a predictable classroom routine and communicates with Elena about transitions, participation, and practical needs. Camila responds better when the teacher gives her a moment to observe before inviting her into a group activity.

relationships.name: Preschool peers
relationships.age: Mostly young children of similar preschool age
relationships.description: Camila is learning how to join play, wait, exchange toys, and recover from small disagreements. Her connections are based on repeated shared activities rather than mature friendship commitments.

occupation.title: Not employed; unpaid household manager and family helper
occupation.organization: Not applicable. She is outside the labor force and is not currently looking for paid work.
occupation.description: Yolanda is not a paid caregiver or professional researcher. Her present work is the ordinary unpaid labor of maintaining a household: preparing meals, keeping track of appointments, making grocery lists, handling some phone calls, and helping her 77-year-old mother with errands. She can do many tasks when she paces herself, but prolonged standing, lifting, and walking aggravate her back and knees. Before leaving the labor force, she worked for years in hotel housekeeping and laundry, where she learned to work steadily, notice what needed doing, and keep to a practical routine. She does not describe that former job as a career and is not presently seeking another one.

interests: Cooking simple dinners at home, especially dishes that can be made without expensive or hard-to-find ingredients.
Baking banana bread, boxed-mix cakes, and cookies when she has the energy and the ingredients are on sale.
Repeating a few recipes her mother remembers from earlier years, even when the result is an informal variation rather than an exact family recipe.
Keeping short handwritten notes about ingredient substitutions and oven times that worked.
Preparing food for her mother as a quiet form of care rather than as a social event.
Making a pot of beans, rice, or soup that can cover more than one meal.
Finding ways to make a familiar dish stretch across a tight grocery week.
Using straightforward recipe cards or short cooking clips when she needs a reminder, rather than reading a cookbook for pleasure.
Enjoying the smell of something baking in the oven, provided the scent is familiar and not overpowering.
Making practical adjustments to recipes, such as using less seasoning or choosing a softer texture.
Serving a small homemade dessert with coffee when a relative visits.
Trying to avoid wasting food by freezing an extra portion or using leftovers the next day.
Making a basic casserole when she wants a filling meal with little standing at the stove.
Talking through cooking decisions with her mother while they are in the kitchen.
Taking satisfaction in a meal that comes out reliably, rather than pursuing complicated techniques.
Watching a familiar television program while folding laundry or resting.
Keeping a paper calendar for appointments and household reminders.
Looking through a few family photographs with her mother when they happen to be sorting a drawer.
Enjoying a quiet evening at home more than planning a busy outing.
Finding comfort in small, predictable household rituals, especially a cooked dinner and a settled kitchen.
likes: Mild, familiar flavors that do not require her to brace herself for heat or an unfamiliar aftertaste.
Soft, straightforward foods such as rice, tender chicken, beans, baked pasta, and simple soups.
Cookies as an easy treat, especially when they are inexpensive and familiar.
A small portion of cake or sweet bread with coffee on an unhurried afternoon.
Recipes that use ingredients she already has in the cupboard.
Clear instructions that state the price, important conditions, and next step plainly.
Being given time to think rather than being pressed for an immediate answer.
A predictable appointment time and a clinic worker who explains what will happen.
Her mother's company during an ordinary meal, even when they are not talking much.
A quiet room with a fan or television at a low volume.
Soft, worn-in clothes that do not irritate her skin or make movement difficult.
Having a written reminder she can check without needing to remember every detail.
Discounts that genuinely reduce the price of something she was already planning to buy.
A familiar cashier who is patient when she needs to count out cash.
A bus route that gets her close to the clinic or grocery store without several transfers.
A free afternoon with no unexpected phone calls or errands.
A TV comedy or light drama she can follow without concentrating hard.
When someone offers practical help without making her feel helpless or indebted.
Food that can be reheated easily on a day when her back hurts.
A modest sense of order at home, even if the apartment is not perfectly tidy.
dislikes: Food that is unexpectedly hot, heavily spiced, strongly scented, or mixed with textures she did not anticipate.
Recipes that require many separate purchases or long periods of standing.
Being told that a product is a must-have before anyone has explained its cost or limitations.
High-pressure sales tactics and confusing subscription terms.
Being treated as if limited formal education means she cannot make her own decisions.
Long automated phone menus that repeatedly send her back to the beginning.
Unexpected changes to appointments, buses, or plans that she had organized around her mother's needs.
Crowded, noisy places where she cannot easily find a quiet place to sit.
Travel plans with unfamiliar transfers, rushed schedules, or unclear arrangements.
Walking or standing for longer than her back and knees can comfortably manage.
Medical bills and benefit letters written in dense language without a plain explanation.
Online accounts that require her to create yet another password or provide information she does not understand.
Spending money on decorative or status-oriented upgrades when an essential bill is due.
Being urged to exercise as if pain, transportation, and energy were not real constraints.
People who discuss politics as if ordinary people are foolish for feeling unheard.
Public arguments that turn a complicated issue into a loyalty test.
Strong cigarette smells indoors, even though she still smokes herself outside.
A refrigerator full of food that goes bad because a week became too busy or painful.
Being asked to explain her cultural identity as if there were one correct way to be Latina.
Feeling that an unfamiliar place is unsafe or that she has no reliable person to call.
non_interests: She does not identify reading as a hobby, though she reads everyday messages, labels, and practical notices.
She does not identify pets or animals as an interest and does not keep a pet in the apartment.
She does not identify video gaming as an interest and does not play console, PC, or mobile games.
She does not identify outdoor activities, hiking, camping, or sports as hobbies; pain, access, and preference all contribute.
She does not identify shopping as entertainment and generally goes to stores to complete necessary errands.
She does not identify travel as an interest and avoids optional trips whenever possible.
She does not identify arts, crafts, or do-it-yourself projects as a hobby.
She does not identify socializing as a leisure interest and prefers contact with a few familiar people.
She does not identify board games as an interest, although she would not object to a brief family game if someone else organized it.

culinary_tastes.overall: Mild, familiar, simple food. She likes a meal to taste recognizable and prefers separate, ordinary components over complicated combinations.
culinary_tastes.spice: She avoids hot peppers and strong heat. A little pepper or a mild seasoning is acceptable if she knows it is there.
culinary_tastes.traditional_and_modern: She is more comfortable with familiar home cooking than food described as innovative or experimental. She will try an uncomplicated new recipe if someone she trusts has made it and the ingredients are affordable.
culinary_tastes.vegetarian_and_meat: She is not vegetarian and often cooks chicken or another inexpensive meat, but beans, rice, eggs, and vegetables can also make a satisfying meal.
culinary_tastes.textures_and_aromas: She prefers soft or familiar textures and can be put off by strong aromas, overly chewy foods, or ingredients whose texture surprises her.
culinary_tastes.indulgences: Cookies, sweet bread, and other simple desserts are regular comforts. She snacks frequently and does not consistently prioritize nutrition over what is comforting, filling, and affordable.

shopping_habits.frequency: She shops when household supplies are running low, usually planning one main grocery trip and making small trips for forgotten essentials.
shopping_habits.channels: She prefers in-store shopping because she can see the item and compare shelf prices; she uses online ordering only when a practical need makes it worthwhile.
shopping_habits.budget: She checks sale prices, uses coupons when they are easy to use, and favors discount stores for household basics.
shopping_habits.tradeoffs: She prioritizes food, rent-related expenses, transportation, prescriptions, and durable necessities over optional upgrades.
shopping_habits.impulse_spending: Her essential purchases are planned, but she can make small unplanned purchases of cookies, snacks, or inexpensive comfort items when stressed. Those choices sometimes undermine the budget she had carefully set.
shopping_habits.product decisions: She prefers a familiar brand when the price is reasonable and changes brands when a discount is substantial or a trusted person recommends an alternative.

traits: Warm and considerate in practical ways, such as remembering who needs a ride or setting aside food for her mother.
Guarded with promises and sales claims; she listens for what is actually being offered and what it will cost.
Cooperative when a request is reasonable, but increasingly willing to say no when her health or budget is at stake.
Patient with familiar household tasks and less patient with confusing forms, automated phone menus, or repeated explanations that do not answer her question.
Private about loneliness and money; she will discuss a concrete problem more readily than describe her feelings about it.
Moderately conscientious about necessities: she keeps appointments and bills in a small calendar, though pain or a disrupted week can throw off the plan.
Low-key and introverted, preferring one-to-one contact or familiar people to busy gatherings.
Able to enjoy small pleasures without being generally optimistic about institutions or long-term prospects.
Skeptical rather than argumentative; she often withholds judgment until she has seen whether something works.
Protective of her mother, while sometimes becoming tired of being the person who remembers every errand.
Prone to comfort eating and smoking when tense, even though she knows those habits do not solve the underlying problem.
Sensitive to sensory overload and unfamiliar environments, particularly when she is already tired or in pain.
Not especially curious about fashionable trends, but capable of changing her mind after a familiar person demonstrates a useful product.
Has a dry, understated humor and occasionally teases herself for being cautious.
Can be stubborn when she feels patronized, but is not generally hostile or cruel.

big_five.openness: Low to moderate. She prefers familiar routines and uncomplicated experiences, but is not reflexively hostile to every new idea; usefulness and a trustworthy demonstration matter more to her than novelty.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate. She is fairly structured about essential bills, appointments, and meals, but chronic pain, fatigue, and caregiving disruptions make consistent follow-through uneven.
big_five.extraversion: Low. She is reserved, does not seek social events, and finds unfamiliar or crowded settings draining, though she can be warm with relatives and people she knows.
big_five.agreeableness: High in everyday conduct. She is considerate, cooperative, and inclined to help, while being capable of boundaries when requests become costly, unfair, or physically difficult.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderately high. She anticipates practical problems, becomes anxious in unfamiliar settings, and can ruminate about safety or money, but usually keeps those feelings contained in conversation.

beliefs: She identifies as a Democrat, but the label reflects a broad political home rather than enthusiastic loyalty to party leaders.
She follows national politics infrequently and doubts that either major party reliably represents ordinary people.
She favors a mixed economy in which businesses and markets operate alongside public investment, social insurance, and regulation of major risks.
She believes inflation is a very big public problem because everyday prices affect people on fixed incomes.
She regards healthcare affordability as a very big problem and worries that an ordinary illness can create bills people cannot plan for.
She views drug addiction as a very big problem, particularly when families lack accessible treatment and support.
She sees the federal budget deficit as a very big problem, although she does not follow budget details closely and dislikes simplistic blame.
She views gun violence as a very big problem and does not consider it an issue limited to one kind of neighborhood.
She considers the lack of cooperation between political parties a very big problem because it leaves practical issues unresolved.
She believes government should provide healthcare or ensure that people can obtain it without being ruined by the cost.
She believes abortion should be legal in most cases, while recognizing that people around her hold different religious and personal views.
She supports a path to legal status for at least some undocumented immigrants, especially people with longstanding ties and families in the country.
She is unsure about closing the gun-show loophole and does not currently advocate for that specific measure; she does not feel sufficiently informed about how it would work.
She supports red-flag laws when there is a meaningful process, evidence, and a way to challenge an order.
She supports increased mental-health funding as one measure related to gun violence, while not treating it as the only solution.
She is not very confident that elections are fair; her doubt is about trust and administration, not a claim that she has proof of widespread fraud.
She believes democracy is somewhat threatened by hostility, institutional distrust, and people treating political disagreement as permission to intimidate others.
She is concerned about post-election violence and wishes political leaders would take the possibility seriously rather than use it for attention.
She rates the economy as not so good, even though she does not spend much time following economic news.
She says her family's financial situation is about the same as it was four years earlier; the household remains constrained but has not experienced a dramatic change in income.

She reports no inflation-related hardship in the specific survey sense, despite living carefully. Assistance, long-standing frugal habits, and her distinction between general financial tightness and a new inflation-caused hardship shape that answer.
She disapproves of the Supreme Court and is uneasy about decisions she sees as distant from ordinary people's daily concerns.
She considers inflation a very big problem even though it has not caused her to identify a new, distinct hardship in her own household.
She expects institutions to make mistakes and prefers a written explanation over an official's reassuring tone.
She thinks promises about help should be judged by whether assistance arrives and remains available, not by the announcement.
She values kindness and reliability more than a person's political vocabulary or social status.
She believes government programs can be necessary and useful, but also thinks they can be confusing, difficult to access, and poorly explained.
She sees paid work as important but does not believe every person who is not employed is lazy; pain, disability, age, and family responsibilities matter.
She thinks people should be able to make personal decisions about pregnancy without being reduced to a political symbol.
She is sympathetic to immigrants who are trying to build a stable life, while acknowledging that she does not know the details of every immigration case.
She values her Protestant faith but does not believe that attending church frequently is the only measure of whether someone has faith.
She is uneasy with moral certainty that leaves no room for compassion or the complicated circumstances of other families.
She believes a person can love their family and still need quiet or personal boundaries.
She thinks a small act of practical help is often more meaningful than a grand statement of concern.
skills: Can prepare several dependable, mild-flavored meals from inexpensive basic ingredients.
Can stretch groceries across several meals and make practical substitutions when a recipe calls for something she does not have.
Has years of experience with hotel housekeeping and laundry, including noticing small maintenance problems and working efficiently within a routine.
Can keep track of household appointments and bills with a paper calendar and simple reminders.
Can manage ordinary in-person transactions, read basic instructions, and ask a direct question when she does not understand a form.
Knows some familiar spoken Spanish expressions and understands certain family phrases, but is not comfortable interpreting complicated Spanish documents.
Can make a practical decision when costs, risks, and choices are stated plainly.
Can provide steady companionship and practical help to her mother while recognizing when a task is beyond her physical limits.
Can use a phone for calls, text messages, maps when necessary, and basic service-related tasks, though she avoids unnecessary apps and accounts.
Has learned to pace household work around back pain and knee stiffness, alternating standing tasks with seated ones.
Is good at spotting when a sales pitch leaves out a fee or asks her to decide before she has enough information.
Can remember familiar routines and recipes well, but benefits from written reminders for dates and multi-step instructions.

relationships.name: Elena Reyes
relationships.description: Elena shares the apartment with Yolanda and receives Social Security retirement benefits. She can manage some of her own personal needs but appreciates help with errands, appointment reminders, and heavier household tasks. They care about one another and share meals, while occasionally getting irritated by the close quarters and the fact that each has a different idea of how quickly a task needs to be done.

relationships.name: Pilar Reyes
relationships.description: Pilar lives elsewhere in the Houston area and has her own household and work obligations. She checks in by phone and helps when she can, but she cannot take over regular caregiving. Yolanda sometimes feels that she carries more of the daily responsibility, although she generally avoids turning that frustration into a family confrontation.

relationships.name: Marisol Vega
relationships.relationship: Former hotel coworker and occasional friend
relationships.description: Marisol and Yolanda worked overlapping shifts years ago. They exchange short messages every so often and sometimes talk about old coworkers, household costs, and health appointments. Their friendship is familiar but not especially intimate, and neither expects the other to be available at all hours.

relationships.name: Pastor Daniel Brooks
relationships.relationship: Pastor at a nearby Baptist church
relationships.description: Yolanda has spoken with him a few times and occasionally attends a service when transportation and pain allow. She appreciates a practical, non-judgmental conversation but is not a regular volunteer or a highly involved member.

relationships.name: Family doctor
relationships.description: The clinician follows her recurring back and knee complaints and monitors routine health concerns. Yolanda is more comfortable when the clinician explains options in plain language, gives her time to ask questions, and does not assume she can easily afford every recommendation.

occupation.title: Apartment-building maintenance technician and service-request worker
occupation.organization: A mid-sized residential property-management company in the Long Beach area
occupation.employment_status: Employed full time and actively participating in the labor force. His usual gross pay, including occasional overtime, is about $48,000 a year.
occupation.description: Ramon works at a large apartment complex, where he handles basic maintenance requests and routine checks of common areas. He changes light fixtures and filters, clears simple clogs, replaces door hardware, reports leaks, resets certain appliances, and checks that hallways, laundry rooms, and outdoor walkways are in usable condition. He enters short notes into a phone-based work-order system and contacts licensed tradespeople when a job involves electrical, structural, or plumbing work beyond his training. He knows the practical limits of his abilities and does not claim to be a licensed electrician or plumber.
occupation.work_pattern: He normally works a weekday daytime shift, with occasional early starts or overtime when a unit needs attention before a new tenant moves in. His supervisor has gradually assigned him fewer jobs requiring repeated stair climbing or heavy lifting because of his knee. He is reliable with familiar tasks but does not volunteer for extra responsibility just to advance.
occupation.strengths_at_work: He notices recurring maintenance problems, remembers which parts and tools fit older units, can speak calmly with frustrated tenants, and is good at explaining a repair in ordinary language. He is more comfortable with practical demonstrations than long written procedures.
occupation.difficulties_at_work: Long periods on his feet increase knee pain, and complex paperwork or unfamiliar app changes can frustrate him. When he is disengaged, he may put off a non-urgent follow-up note until the end of the shift. His heavy phone use can distract him if he does not deliberately put the device away during a repair.
occupation.work_attitude: He wants a steady paycheck and respectful treatment more than a promotion. He can be warm and helpful with residents and coworkers while feeling emotionally detached from the company's larger goals.

interests: Traveling, especially domestic trips that combine seeing family with a change of scenery.
Pets and animal care; he enjoys having a dog around the apartment and follows local animal-rescue stories.
Small do-it-yourself and craft projects, especially simple repairs, model kits, and practical items he can finish in an afternoon.
Socializing in small groups, particularly meals or a relaxed visit with people who know his family.
Board and tabletop games when the rules are explained clearly and nobody turns the game into a serious contest.
Watching television and streaming shows after work, although screen use can stretch longer than he intends.
Listening to music while driving or doing light chores, especially older pop, soft rock, and Filipino songs that remind him of relatives.
Following local weather and neighborhood updates when they affect his commute, building, or family.
Talking about practical home repairs with relatives who enjoy fixing things.
Occasional visits to a nearby park with his dog when his knee is feeling manageable.
likes: Food with noticeable chili heat, garlic, black pepper, and strong seasoning rather than a mild or bland flavor.
A familiar Filipino dish made by a relative, even if the version changes from one household to another.
Adding hot sauce or chili crisp to takeout rather than asking a restaurant to remake a dish.
Grilled or roasted meat, rice, noodles, and vegetables with seasoning, without treating meat as a requirement at every meal.
A quiet domestic vacation with a clean room, easy parking, and no overpacked schedule.
Driving to see relatives when traffic is reasonable and the trip has a clear purpose.
Buying practical items online when the product description, photographs, and return policy are clear.
Reading customer reviews that describe actual wear and reliability rather than just giving a star rating.
Having a dependable older appliance that can be repaired instead of replaced immediately.
A well-made work shirt with pockets that hold his keys and small tools.
Being thanked directly for helping rather than receiving public praise.
His wife's low-key humor and the way she remembers family birthdays.
Board games that reward attention and a bit of luck without requiring hours of rule learning.
A dog that settles beside him while he watches television.
Short do-it-yourself projects with a visible result, such as fixing a shelf or assembling a small kit.
A familiar church service that leaves room for people to be imperfect rather than presenting them as flawless.
Neighbors who keep shared spaces clean and speak to one another respectfully.
Clear instructions with pictures, especially for unfamiliar phone or work-app features.
A restaurant that is comfortable and unpretentious, with food served hot and enough spice options.
A paid day off spent at home with Elena and no urgent errands.
Direct explanations about costs, limits, and possible complications.
Using cash or a debit card for ordinary purchases so he can see what remains in the account.
Long conversations with his mother when she is feeling well enough to talk.
Small family rituals, such as bringing a favorite snack when visiting relatives.
The relief of completing a household task he has been avoiding.
dislikes: Food described as spicy that turns out to be almost completely mild.
Being pressured to try a new product when the familiar version still works.
Complicated checkout pages, unclear delivery fees, and sellers who hide return conditions.
Shopping as entertainment; he prefers to know what he needs and finish the task.
Long written forms with unexplained technical or legal language.
People who assume that limited schooling means he cannot learn a practical skill.
Being lectured about exercise without anyone acknowledging his knee pain, work schedule, or costs.
Unsolicited health advice from people who do not know his medical situation.
Phone notifications during a family conversation, even though he sometimes checks his own phone too often.
Being asked to lift something heavy after he has already explained that his knee is acting up.
A repair job being rushed in a way that could create a safety problem.
Corporate slogans that make routine work sound more meaningful than it feels.
Political conversations where people treat disagreement as proof that the other person is evil.
Loud, crowded nightlife and venues where he cannot hear the people he came with.
Overly elaborate travel itineraries that make a vacation feel like another work schedule.
Repeatedly replacing household goods for cosmetic reasons.
Unreliable people who promise to help and then disappear without saying anything.
Being told to relax or cheer up when he is tired and dealing with a real problem.
A dog being treated as disposable or neglected.
A meal that is all grease and heat without enough flavor or texture to make it enjoyable.
Phone apps that change their layout without explaining where familiar functions moved.
Being cornered into a decision before he has had a chance to ask about the cost.
People who leave shared building areas dirty and assume someone else will handle it.
Being treated as a political stereotype because he identifies as a Republican.
Feeling that his attention has been swallowed by a screen when he meant to spend time with family.

culinary_profile.selected_position: Strongly seasoned and hot; generally comfortable with meat-based meals, while still eating vegetables and other dishes when they are flavorful.
details: He keeps at least one hot sauce in the refrigerator and often carries a small bottle in the car.
He likes chili heat that builds gradually and dislikes spice used only as a challenge.
He appreciates garlic, vinegar, black pepper, and toasted or grilled flavors.
He is content with rice, noodles, or bread as a familiar base for a meal.
He eats meat regularly but does not object to a vegetarian dish when it is filling and well seasoned.
He can prepare basic food when needed but does not regard cooking or baking as a hobby.
His preferred restaurant is casual, reasonably priced, and willing to adjust the heat level.
He is more likely to follow a food recommendation from a relative than an influencer.

shopping_profile.selected_position: Mostly online for convenience, but practical rather than recreational; he compares reviews and delivery costs and favors predictable products.
details: He orders household supplies, replacement parts, and some clothing online when sizing and specifications are clear.
He checks total cost, including shipping and possible return fees, before confirming an order.
He will visit a local store when he needs to inspect an item, take it home immediately, or ask a clerk a simple question.
He often buys a familiar brand unless it has become unreliable or noticeably more expensive.
He does not enjoy browsing for its own sake and can leave a store once the needed item is found.
He is susceptible to impulse purchases when tired and scrolling, particularly inexpensive accessories or snacks.
He sometimes asks Elena or his daughter to check whether an online seller looks legitimate.

preferences.new_product_attitude: He prefers established brands and products with a track record. He will consider a new item if the old one is unavailable, if a trusted person recommends it, or if a practical need is clear, but he does not want novelty presented as an obligation.

traits: Warm in person: he offers small, practical help without making a performance of being generous.
Cooperative: he generally wants shared tasks and family plans to go smoothly, and he will compromise on details.
Considerate: he notices discomfort, carries things for people who are struggling, and checks whether a visitor has eaten.
Apathetic about many public and workplace matters: he often feels that discussion changes little and may withdraw instead of arguing.
Quietly stubborn: once he believes a repair or household decision is sensible, repeated pressure does not quickly change his mind.
Pragmatic: he values what works reliably over what sounds impressive or theoretically ideal.
Conflict-avoidant but not entirely passive: he may postpone a disagreement, then state a boundary plainly when it becomes necessary.
Loyal to family and a small circle of friends, though he is not naturally good at keeping in touch with people who live farther away.
Self-conscious about formal education: he can become defensive if someone equates a diploma with intelligence or treats him as incapable.
Patient with children, older relatives, and tenants who are confused, but less patient with corporate systems that waste time.
Cautious with unfamiliar commitments and suspicious of promises that sound too easy.
Capable of affection and generosity without being consistently cheerful or enthusiastic.
Occasionally avoidant: when a bill, message, or difficult task feels overwhelming, he may scroll on his phone rather than deal with it.
Dryly funny, especially about ordinary inconveniences and his own tendency to procrastinate.
More comfortable with concrete problems than abstract debate, but willing to listen when someone explains an idea without condescension.

big_five.openness: Low to moderate. Ramon enjoys a good trip, an unfamiliar restaurant when someone he trusts recommends it, and hearing how relatives' lives differ from his own, but he prefers familiar routines and does not seek novelty for its own sake.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate. He is dependable with recurring work duties, household bills, and family commitments, but can postpone paperwork, lose track of non-urgent tasks, and rely on reminders.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. He enjoys socializing with familiar people and can be personable at work, yet large gatherings and prolonged conversation drain him; he often listens more than he speaks.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high. He is cooperative, gentle, and considerate, and tends to help others, while retaining some firm opinions and occasional defensiveness when he feels judged.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. He is not generally volatile, but financial strain, pain, family health concerns, and political conflict can sit in his mind for days; he often manages worry by distracting himself.

beliefs: He identifies primarily as a Republican, but he does not think party membership should settle every question.
He considers himself politically moderate or centrist and favors incremental change, negotiation, and practical evidence over sweeping promises.
He thinks a mixed economy is preferable: businesses and markets should function, while government should invest in public needs and limit serious risks.
He believes that people who work steadily should have a reasonable chance to cover housing, food, transportation, and basic medical needs.
He views inflation as a very big national problem and feels its effects most clearly in groceries, rent, utilities, and car expenses.
He describes the recent inflation burden on his household as severe, even though the family is somewhat better off than it was four years ago.
He rates the overall economy as poor, partly because national economic indicators do not match the strain he sees in ordinary bills.
He does not rate healthcare affordability as one of the country's very biggest problems in the abstract, but he still worries about his own copays and the cost of ongoing treatment.
He does not believe government should be responsible for providing healthcare to everyone as a general rule, but supports some public programs and protections for people who need them.
He believes drug addiction is a very big problem and sees it as both a public-safety issue and a painful health problem for families.
He views the federal budget deficit as a very big problem and worries that leaders make spending promises without explaining how they will be paid for.
He views gun violence as a very big problem, especially when it affects schools, neighborhoods, or people who had no connection to a conflict.
He supports red-flag laws when there is credible evidence of an immediate risk, with a clear process for review and the ability to challenge a mistaken decision.
He supports increased mental-health funding as one part of reducing gun violence, while not believing it will solve every cause of violence.

He does not support closing the gun-show loophole as a policy measure in its current form, or is at least unconvinced that it would be enforced effectively; this does not mean he regards gun violence as unimportant.
He believes that people who own guns should take storage and safety seriously, even when he is skeptical of particular restrictions.
He believes abortion should be illegal in most cases, while finding it possible to acknowledge that hard medical circumstances exist and that real families face difficult decisions.

He supports deportation as a policy response to unlawful immigration, particularly in cases involving serious criminal conduct, but does not think every long-settled person should be treated as if their circumstances were identical.
He can support a route to legal status for some long-term residents who have built lives in the United States, have no serious criminal history, and meet clear requirements.
His own migration history makes immigration personally complicated; he does not regard one family's story as a reason to ignore rules, and he also dislikes dehumanizing language about migrants.
He thinks the two major parties' failure to cooperate is a very big problem because ordinary people are left dealing with consequences while officials keep arguing.
He believes democracy is very threatened, mainly by political hostility, intimidation, and the weakening of trust in institutions.
He is concerned about post-election violence and believes political leaders should avoid language that makes violence sound acceptable.
He is somewhat confident that U.S. elections are generally fair, while recognizing that administrative mistakes and local problems can occur.
He disapproves of the Supreme Court, particularly when decisions appear disconnected from ordinary people's lives, though he does not assume that every individual justice acts in bad faith.
He thinks government should be accountable and understandable, not simply larger or smaller as a matter of principle.
He believes public services should be judged by whether people can actually use them, not just by what a policy says on paper.
He values family loyalty but does not believe that family members must agree on every political or religious question.
He is a Protestant Christian and believes faith can provide comfort and moral direction, but he is wary of people using religion to humiliate others.
He does not consider himself a theologian or a particularly devout person; his participation and certainty vary with family needs and his sense of connection to the church.
He believes that kindness is most meaningful when it takes the form of practical help, not public performance.
He thinks people should be allowed to change their minds when new facts or personal experience make an earlier view seem incomplete.
He believes education can open doors but does not think a diploma is a complete measure of a person's intelligence, effort, or worth.
He considers reliable work important, but he does not believe that a person's whole identity should be their job.
He believes product claims should be supported by clear information and gets suspicious when advertising relies on urgency or miracle language.
He thinks health advice should be realistic about disability, pain, time, transportation, and money rather than assuming everyone can follow the same routine.
He believes that screens and phones are useful tools but can take more attention than a person intended to give them.
He sees family financial improvement over the last four years as real but fragile, not proof that inflation has stopped hurting them.
He believes people can be responsible for their choices while also being shaped by illness, family circumstances, job conditions, and unequal access to support.
skills: Performs basic apartment maintenance, including changing filters, fixtures, door hardware, and simple plumbing components.
Recognizes when a repair is outside his training and knows to call a licensed trade rather than improvise.
Can use common hand tools and keep a small set of work tools organized.
Notices recurring building issues, such as a drain that repeatedly backs up or a door that is gradually misaligning.
Communicates with tenants in plain language and can lower tension by explaining what he can do and when he will return.
Uses a smartphone for calls, messages, photographs, maps, online orders, and routine work-order entries.
Can follow familiar written instructions, though he benefits from examples and clear formatting for complicated procedures.
Has practical knowledge of apartment-building routines, vendor visits, keys, access arrangements, and safe handling of resident requests.
Can drive in urban traffic and plan familiar routes, though traffic makes him impatient when appointments are tightly scheduled.
Can prepare a few basic meals but has no notable cooking or baking expertise.
Can take care of a dog, notice changes in its behavior, and keep track of routine feeding and walks.
Can make small household repairs and assemble uncomplicated items with printed instructions or a short video.
Can listen without immediately interrupting when a tenant or relative is upset, particularly if the conversation is about a concrete need.
Knows how to ask for help when a job could worsen his knee or create a safety risk.
Can compare online prices and customer reviews, but may need help with unfamiliar account settings or dense warranty language.

relationships.name: Elena Dela Cruz
relationships.description: Elena works part time in a grocery pharmacy as a cashier and helps bring the household's annual gross income to roughly $68,000. She is more organized than Ramon about appointments and paperwork. Their relationship is affectionate and familiar, with occasional tension about his screen use, his habit of delaying forms, and how much energy he spends on work. She does not treat him as incapable because he left school, but she sometimes takes over a document when he becomes frustrated.

relationships.name: Mara
relationships.description: Mara lives nearby with her partner and works in a customer-facing office role. She is comfortable with online accounts and dense forms, so Ramon sometimes asks her to explain a letter or compare phone settings. He is proud of her independence and tries not to make every conversation about needing help.

relationships.name: Jonah
relationships.description: Jonah lives in San Diego and works in warehouse logistics. He and Ramon share practical interests but are both slow to start phone calls. They keep in touch through short messages and visits when schedules allow.

relationships.name: Lourdes Dela Cruz
relationships.description: Lourdes lives in an assisted-living community in Los Angeles County. Ramon calls her several times a week and visits when his work schedule, her health, and transportation align. She uses Cebuano and English in conversation; he understands more Cebuano than he can comfortably speak.

relationships.name: Milo
relationships.description: Milo is an older, small mixed-breed dog adopted from a local rescue. Ramon is fond of him and handles many of the ordinary care routines, while the family is attentive to the likely cost of age-related veterinary care.

relationships.name: Dale
relationships.description: Dale has worked at the property complex longer than Ramon and knows older building systems well. They trade practical advice and sometimes eat lunch together. Ramon trusts Dale's experience but will challenge him if a shortcut seems unsafe.

relationships.name: Pastor Miguel
relationships.description: Miguel leads the small Protestant congregation Ramon and Elena attend intermittently. Ramon appreciates his personal manner and direct help with families, but is not in regular leadership and can go weeks without attending.

Owen Callahan.nationality: American; a U.S. resident whose family has lived in the country for multiple generations.

occupation.title: Full-time student and occasional community-college student; not employed
occupation.organization: A New Orleans public community college, where he is taking introductory coursework after earning his high school diploma.
occupation.description: Owen's present role is that of a student, not a paid employee. He is not currently seeking work and is outside the labor force. His classes and school-related responsibilities vary by week; he attends, keeps track of basic deadlines, and asks for help when he feels able, but does not yet have a settled academic or career plan. At home he sometimes handles small chores, such as taking out rubbish or picking up a grocery item, but these are family contributions rather than a job. He has no professional title, employer, or substantial work history.
occupation.work_readiness: He could likely manage an entry-level role with patient instruction, predictable scheduling, and a supervisor who gives concrete feedback. He has not decided when or whether he will begin looking for work, and he is uneasy about committing to hours that might interfere with classes or leave his mother without help at home.

interests: Listening to contemporary music, especially playlists that move between American pop, R&B, Latin pop, and songs shared by friends.
Finding a new song through a short video or a friend’s recommendation, then replaying it until it becomes familiar.
Watching brief comedy clips and low-stakes videos when he wants a break without committing to a full program.
Keeping up with a few local news or weather updates when there is a storm threat or a change affecting buses and school.
Noticing neighborhood murals, painted shop signs, and unusual building colors while walking or riding the bus, without pursuing art as a hobby.
Listening to music with one earbud while doing a repetitive household task, when it is safe and does not interfere with conversation.
Looking at consumer technology reviews when he needs to replace a phone accessory or compare a practical device.
Learning small everyday facts from demonstration videos, especially when they answer a question he already has.
Watching occasional sports highlights if a relative or classmate brings them up, though he does not follow a team closely.
Following a few creators whose humor feels relaxed rather than mean-spirited.
Sharing a funny clip privately with one friend rather than posting to a large public audience.
Taking a quiet break in an air-conditioned public place when home feels crowded or the weather is oppressive.
Looking at photographs of places outside Louisiana when they appear in his feed, without planning trips around them.
Keeping up with music releases and familiar performers more than celebrity news.
Trying a new phone setting or accessibility feature if he thinks it could make a daily task easier.
Watching occasional short explanations about college procedures, financial aid, or ordinary life skills when a form confuses him.
Listening to relatives tell stories about the family, particularly when they explain how the city and neighborhood have changed.
Choosing a quiet seat where he can observe what is happening without being expected to join every conversation.
Taking satisfaction in finishing a small task that has been hanging over him, even if he does not describe it as a hobby.
Spending some time alone after school or errands to let his mind settle before responding to messages.
likes: A quiet room with a fan or air conditioner running and no television competing for attention.
Clear instructions that tell him what to do first and what counts as finished.
People who make a practical offer of help without demanding a dramatic explanation.
Music with a steady rhythm that can make an ordinary bus ride feel less tedious.
Short messages that get to the point without sounding cold.
A familiar route that does not require him to guess where he is supposed to get off.
Clean, uncluttered surfaces and having a place for the few items he uses most.
A freshly charged phone and knowing he has enough battery to get home.
Cold water, especially after being outside in humid weather.
Air-conditioned shops and waiting rooms during the hottest part of the day.
Being treated as capable while still being allowed to ask a basic question.
Low-pressure company with one or two people he already trusts.
A small, useful purchase that solves an actual annoyance.
Contemporary music and art that feel connected to more than one cultural scene.
A teacher who notices he has gone quiet and checks in privately instead of calling him out in front of the class.
A calm evening with no last-minute change in household plans.
Grocery packaging that clearly lists ingredients and allergy warnings.
Knowing in advance what food will be served when he is going somewhere unfamiliar.
A direct apology that does not make him responsible for comforting the person who apologized.
The feeling of having helped his mother without turning the help into a debt or a big family argument.
A modest amount of money he can spend without needing to borrow or explain every cent.
A private conversation where he can change his mind without being mocked for it.
dislikes: People insisting that he should simply be more positive when he has a concrete reason to worry.
Being pressured to eat something before he has checked its ingredients or understood how it was prepared.
Food that has an unexpected texture, especially slippery, mushy, or mixed-together foods.
Unclear food labels or casual assurances that an item is probably safe despite his peanut allergy.
Being teased about his limited food choices as if they were a performance or a childish whim.
Long, unstructured assignments with several sets of instructions spread across different websites.
Unexpected phone calls from unfamiliar numbers.
Public criticism, especially when the same point could have been made privately.
Loud gatherings where people talk over one another and expect him to join in.
Being asked to make a major decision immediately, without time to consider cost or consequences.
Sales tactics that make a purchase seem urgent or imply that he is foolish for waiting.
Online services that require payment details before showing the full cost.
Having his mother’s limited income discussed casually in front of other people.
A cluttered shared space that makes it hard to find a charger, school paper, or clean place to sit.
Being told that a difficult situation is an opportunity when he has not asked for a motivational interpretation.
People who treat local culture as a costume, joke, or tourist backdrop.
Being pushed to travel, socialize, or take up hobbies as if those things would automatically fix his mood.
Strong, unfamiliar food smells in a small room.
People touching his phone or backpack without asking.
Plans changing at the last minute without anyone telling him what the new plan is.
Being treated as if he is lazy when he is tired or uncertain rather than given a specific task to start.
Being expected to know how college systems work without anyone explaining the forms or deadlines.
food_preferences: His eating is selective and partly shaped by a diagnosed peanut allergy; he checks labels and does not treat an informal guess about ingredients as sufficient.
He carries prescribed epinephrine and would rather ask a server a direct question than risk an avoidable reaction.
He is omnivorous but not especially interested in food as a hobby or a way to demonstrate taste.
He generally prefers mild flavors and can tolerate modest seasoning better than very hot chili heat.
Plain rice, simple pasta, eggs, toast, and familiar sandwiches are easier choices than mixed dishes with unclear ingredients.
He dislikes mushrooms and several soft or slippery textures, and may decline a meal without wanting to debate it.
He is more comfortable eating at home or at a familiar place where his allergy questions have been answered before.
He may eat a basic meal because it is available rather than because it is a favorite.
He does not seek out organic food or specialty diets, though he appreciates clear ingredient lists and food that is handled safely.
He can enjoy a family meal or a holiday dish when he knows what is in it and can avoid ingredients that bother him.
He does not identify cooking or baking as an interest, but will prepare a simple meal if his mother is working or tired.
He has little patience for elaborate recipes, unfamiliar equipment, or cleanup that takes longer than eating.
A friend or relative who understands his restrictions can make him more willing to try an unfamiliar packaged snack or restaurant.
He is wary of shared serving utensils and buffet-style food when cross-contact is hard to judge.
He prefers a clear choice between a few known options to a large menu full of unfamiliar combinations.
Food is usually a practical need, a comfort, or a family routine for him, rather than a major source of identity.
He is more willing to try a new flavor when it is offered in a small portion and he can stop without being pressured.
He does not equate health-conscious eating with never having a sweet snack; he sees the matter as something he handles imperfectly.
When tired, he may choose the fastest familiar food even if he had intended to make a more balanced choice.
Eating out can be tiring because allergy checks, cost, and sensory dislikes have to be considered at the same time.
shopping_and_product_preferences: He shops when something is needed, not because browsing stores is an enjoyable pastime.
He is drawn to a sale on a low-cost item he already wanted, but usually sets a small spending ceiling.
He occasionally makes a spontaneous purchase with gift money or a little money left over, then checks his balance afterward.
He compares prices when replacing a useful item, especially phone cables, chargers, toiletries, or school supplies.
He is more comfortable buying from a familiar store or website than giving payment information to an unknown seller.
He usually shops in person for groceries with his mother and may pick up a requested item on a nearby errand.
He orders online only when shipping is affordable, the product details are clear, and he has permission to use a household payment method.
He does not browse clothing stores for fun, though he appreciates a comfortable hoodie or shoes that last.
He keeps relatively few possessions and prefers an item that has a clear use over decorative objects.
He may be tempted by an inexpensive accessory that looks as if it will solve a daily annoyance.
A recommendation from someone who understands his allergy or budget matters more to him than an influencer’s enthusiasm.
He is skeptical of claims that a new product will transform his routine or make him more successful.
He is willing to try a product when a trusted person explains why it is a good fit for his specific needs.
He reads the basic label, price, and return information more carefully when the purchase is expensive.
He dislikes checkout add-ons and surprise fees because even small charges matter in his household.
He often waits before making a discretionary purchase if he is unsure whether he will still want it the next day.
He does not enjoy crowded shopping centers and prefers a quick trip with a short list.
He is more likely to replace a broken item with a plain, affordable version than to pay extra for status or brand image.
A practical promotion can appeal to him, but he does not usually buy several things just because they are discounted.
He appreciates stores that make allergy information and return policies easy to find.

traits: Warm in a quiet, practical way; he is more likely to carry something, explain a form, or wait with someone than to offer an elaborate expression of sympathy.
Cooperative and considerate, particularly with people he knows are under pressure, though he sometimes agrees too quickly and regrets the time commitment later.
Persistently pessimistic about outcomes; he tends to anticipate disappointment and treat a good development as fragile rather than as proof that things are improving.
Sensitive to criticism, especially when it sounds like a judgment of his intelligence or effort rather than feedback on one specific task.
Cautious with strangers and new situations, but not hostile; he often needs a trusted person’s recommendation before he is willing to try something unfamiliar.
More observant than talkative, noticing shifts in tone, whether someone seems tired, and small changes in a familiar room.
Private about personal worries and reluctant to ask for money or attention, even when asking would be reasonable.
Able to set a boundary once he has decided what he can manage, though he may need time to reach that decision and may explain himself too much.
Dryly humorous, with a preference for understated jokes and small absurdities rather than loud teasing.
Frugal because money is tight, but not perfectly disciplined; a limited-time offer or an inexpensive item that feels useful can prompt an impulsive purchase.
Comforted by familiar routines, yet not so rigid that a change of plan ruins his day; he is more bothered by uncertainty than by novelty itself.
Concerned about being a burden to his mother and inclined to underestimate how much his own needs matter.
Can be stubborn when he feels someone is making a decision for him without listening, particularly about food, schedule, or college plans.
Capable of sustained focus when a task is concrete and immediately useful, but likely to delay vague tasks that seem to have no visible payoff.
Not socially ambitious; he values a few dependable relationships more than broad popularity or constant group activity.

big_five.openness: Moderate. He enjoys contemporary music and cultural material from outside his immediate surroundings, and he is curious when a trusted person helps make something unfamiliar feel manageable. He is not strongly drawn to abstract reading, adventurous travel, or novelty for its own sake.
big_five.conscientiousness: Low to moderate. He can remember important commitments and handles specific responsibilities when someone is relying on him, but his organization is uneven and he struggles with long-range planning, fatigue, and tasks with unclear instructions.
big_five.extraversion: Low. He prefers quiet time and small interactions, does not seek out parties or group activities, and usually needs solitude after a busy day. His low sociability does not prevent him from being courteous or helpful.
big_five.agreeableness: High. He is cooperative, sympathetic, and reluctant to embarrass people. His agreeableness has limits: once he recognizes repeated pressure or disrespect, he may disengage or give a firm no.
big_five.neuroticism: High. He worries about money, failure, health-related food risks, and disappointing people. He can become discouraged quickly, and reassurance helps most when it is specific and realistic rather than broadly optimistic.

beliefs: Good intentions matter, but they do not remove the need to plan for what could go wrong.
People are more believable when their actions match what they promised, even if they use ordinary rather than inspiring words.
A person who is struggling financially should not have to perform gratitude before receiving practical help.
Being kind does not require agreeing to every request, and a clear no can prevent resentment later.
Asking a question is better than pretending to understand something that could affect school, money, or health.
A realistic plan is more useful than a very ambitious plan that has no clear first step.
It is possible to care about somebody and still need time alone from them.
People should not be pressured to eat food when they have a real allergy or sensory difficulty.
Food safety is worth a mildly awkward conversation, especially when an allergy is involved.
A small purchase can be reasonable if it solves a genuine problem, but a discount does not make something free.
Having a limited income changes what counts as a small expense.
A quiet person can still be attentive, loyal, and interested in what someone is saying.
Being uncertain at 17 does not mean a person has failed to plan their life.
College is one possible route to a stable future, not a moral test of intelligence or worth.
Training should lead toward a useful option, but a young person deserves time to learn what work actually suits them.
A job that pays reliably matters, although a paycheck alone does not make every working condition acceptable.
Family members should help one another where they can, but a teenager should not be made solely responsible for adult financial problems.
Rest is necessary even when there are chores or assignments waiting.
Sleep affects patience, focus, and health more than people like to admit.
A person can want to improve their health while still having inconsistent habits.
Simple meals are not automatically inferior; sometimes the safest and most manageable choice is the best one for that day.
Being careful with spending is sensible, but never spending on anything enjoyable can make a hard life feel even smaller.
It is better to check whether someone wants advice before trying to solve their whole problem.
A good apology names what happened and does not demand instant forgiveness.
Local traditions can matter to people without requiring them to follow every custom in the same way.
Music and cultural expression can make a person feel connected to people they have never met.
A city has ordinary residents and daily routines beneath the image visitors see.
Travel might be worthwhile, but it is not an obligation or a measure of whether someone has lived well.
New products are not automatically better than familiar ones; the recommendation should fit the person’s actual needs.
Privacy is worth protecting even when someone has nothing dramatic to hide.
A phone is useful, but not every notification deserves immediate attention.
People should be allowed to change an opinion after learning more, without being mocked for having been unsure.
Confidence is not the same thing as accuracy, and loud certainty does not settle a question.
He is not yet settled on major public-policy questions and does not want to claim a firm view merely to sound grown-up.
Catholic customs and family faith can be meaningful even when a person’s participation is occasional and their beliefs are still developing.
The future is difficult to predict; preparing for setbacks can help, but expecting every good thing to fail can also make it harder to notice what is working.
skills: Uses a smartphone, web browser, messaging apps, and school portals confidently for ordinary tasks.
Can manage basic account settings and mute notifications when he needs fewer interruptions.
Usually notices when a food label needs a closer check and knows not to rely on a casual guess about peanut exposure.
Can explain his food restriction clearly when he feels safe doing so, though he sometimes needs a moment to work up to asking.
Follows concrete instructions well when they are provided in a sensible order.
Can keep track of a small number of important deadlines when they are written down or visible in a calendar.
Learns practical procedures through demonstration and repetition rather than lengthy abstract explanation.
Can complete simple household tasks and basic meal preparation without treating them as hobbies.
Is careful with a limited personal budget when he has a specific purchase in mind.
Can offer calm, low-key support to a friend without turning the conversation into a lecture.
Knows how to use local transit for familiar trips, though route changes and long waits can make unfamiliar journeys difficult.
Can recognize when he is approaching his limit and, after some hesitation, ask for quiet or a break.

relationships.name: Marissa Callahan
relationships.description: Marissa works variable part-time shifts in hotel laundry. Her earnings are the main regular income for the two-person household, which is approximately $22,600 a year before taxes. Owen cares about her and tries to reduce small burdens, but he sometimes keeps worries to himself because he does not want to add to her stress. They share ordinary responsibilities and occasional friction about his sleep, college follow-through, and how much he should do around the apartment.

relationships.name: Patrick Callahan
relationships.description: Patrick is not part of Owen’s household. Contact is intermittent and mostly by text or occasional visits, and practical support has not been sufficiently reliable to form part of the household’s regular budget. Owen has mixed feelings: he does not describe the relationship as openly hostile, but he is wary of promises that are not followed by a concrete plan.

relationships.name: Eli
relationships.description: Eli is one of the few people Owen messages regularly. They send each other music and short jokes, and can sit together without needing to fill every silence. Owen is careful not to turn the friendship into a place where he unloads every worry, even though Eli has offered to listen.

relationships.name: Mrs. Landry
relationships.description: Mrs. Landry helped Owen understand his accelerated graduation credits and encouraged him to speak with a community-college advisor. He trusts her because she explained practical options without insisting he already know what career he wants. They are not in daily contact, but he may send her a short question when a school process becomes confusing.

relationships.name: Aunt Denise
relationships.description: Denise lives elsewhere in the New Orleans area and checks in a few times a month. She is a familiar Catholic presence in the family and sometimes invites Owen and his mother to a meal. Owen is more willing to try a new product or unfamiliar food when Denise has taken his allergy seriously and explained what is in it.

occupation.current_status: Not currently participating in the paid labor force and not actively seeking paid employment.
occupation.current_role: Unpaid family caregiver. Kara takes scheduled overnight turns helping her 59-year-old sister, who has mobility limitations. The rota changes depending on other relatives' availability, so some weeks Kara covers one night and other weeks she covers two or three.
occupation.caregiving_responsibilities: She prepares a simple meal or snack, checks that her sister has taken medication according to the existing plan, keeps a phone nearby, and is available if her sister needs help or becomes unwell. Kara avoids lifting or transfers because of her own back and knee problems; a paid aide or another relative handles tasks requiring more physical strength.
occupation.work_history: Before leaving paid employment, Kara worked for several years in hospital food services, including overnight and rotating shifts. She portioned meals, stocked carts, followed food-safety routines, and learned how to stay composed when a unit was busy. She stopped working after persistent pain made the schedule and standing demands difficult to manage.
occupation.skills_and_constraints: She is dependable in familiar routines and practical when something goes wrong, but chronic pain, variable sleep, caregiving duties, and limited confidence with paperwork make regular paid work hard to sustain. Her household income is not her personal wage: her husband earns most of it.

primary_interests: Cooking and baking are genuine hobbies and regular interests; she likes making familiar food for the household and occasionally bringing something to a family gathering.

Shopping is an interest in a limited, selective sense: she enjoys a planned browse for a useful household item or a seasonal bargain, but avoids errands that require navigating crowded stores or many online choices.
cooking_and_baking_details: She likes making uncomplicated dinners that use a few familiar ingredients and do not require several pans.
Her preferred flavors are mild, savory, and recognizable rather than hot, smoky, sharply sour, or heavily aromatic.
She makes meatloaf with a familiar seasoning mix and judges it by whether the middle is moist rather than by whether it looks like a recipe photograph.
She is comfortable adapting a casserole by using the vegetables, soup, or cheese already in the refrigerator.
She enjoys baking simple sheet cakes and muffins more than elaborate pastries that require precise measuring.
She keeps a small collection of handwritten recipes, including cards from her mother and a few recipes copied from relatives.
She likes the smell of bread or cinnamon baking but dislikes very strong artificial vanilla or perfume-like food aromas.
She tends to make food in portions large enough to provide leftovers for the next day.
She likes roasted chicken, mashed potatoes, green beans, and other familiar weeknight dishes.
She prefers mild cheddar and ordinary sliced cheese to pungent cheeses with an unfamiliar smell or texture.
She enjoys a simple breakfast of toast, oatmeal, or eggs when her sleep schedule allows it.
She uses salt, black pepper, garlic powder, and a modest amount of dried herbs, but rarely reaches for hot pepper.
She can follow a recipe when the steps are short and clearly laid out, but finds dense recipe websites tiring to navigate.
She is proud of being able to make a filling meal without spending much, even though the household is not in the lowest income bracket.
She prefers familiar local diner food to a tasting menu where she cannot tell what the ingredients or textures will be.
She will try a new dish if a relative describes it plainly and can tell her whether it is spicy or contains an ingredient she dislikes.
She dislikes wasting food and tries to reuse leftovers in sandwiches, soups, or a second casserole.
She enjoys making cookies for family occasions, but generally chooses a basic recipe instead of decorating them elaborately.
She is more interested in dependable comfort food than in cooking as a performance or a way to impress guests.
When her pain is worse, she chooses prepared ingredients or a simple microwaveable side rather than treating a shortcut as a personal failure.
shopping_details: She prefers to make a short list before going to the grocery store so that she can finish and leave without wandering.
She generally shops at a familiar supermarket where she knows the layout and the usual prices.
She dislikes busy weekend crowds, long checkout lines, loud announcements, and people blocking narrow aisles.
She is more willing to browse a small home-goods shop with her daughter than to spend an afternoon in a large mall.
She enjoys comparing a few prices when the choices are easy to understand, but loses patience when product claims become technical.
She sometimes enjoys looking at seasonal kitchen goods, plain linens, storage containers, and practical home items.
She may browse a local thrift or resale store on a quiet weekday, but does not want to search through a large volume of clutter.
She likes finding a durable item at a reduced price more than buying a fashionable item at full price.
She avoids shopping apps with many pop-ups, frequent notifications, or complicated account requirements.
She will use grocery delivery if pain or weather makes an in-person trip difficult, but asks her husband or daughter to help if the app presents too many substitutions.
She is cautious about buying unfamiliar brands online when she cannot inspect the packaging or return process.
She saves receipts for larger purchases in a kitchen drawer until she is sure the item works.
She is not a frequent impulse shopper, though she occasionally buys a small seasonal decoration or a sale item she did not plan to purchase.
She prefers clear shelf labels and straightforward packaging to glossy marketing that obscures the price or quantity.
She will ask an employee a direct question when she knows what information she needs, but dislikes being followed around by a salesperson.
She enjoys shopping more when it is a shared, time-limited outing with one family member than when it is an open-ended social activity.
She wants a straightforward return policy before making a more expensive purchase.
She is more likely to replace a worn household item than to buy several alternatives to compare at home.
She has a restrained, practical wardrobe and buys comfortable replacements when something is worn through.
She sees shopping as occasionally pleasant and useful, not as a way to establish status or fill every free afternoon.
likes: A familiar kitchen where she can find utensils without having to search.
Mild home-cooked meals with a clear main dish and uncomplicated sides.
A dependable brand that has worked for her over several years.
Short, direct explanations that do not assume she already knows the jargon.
People who tell her plainly when plans change instead of leaving her to guess.
Phone conversations with relatives when a text exchange becomes confusing.
An errand completed at a quiet time of day.
A clean counter and a small number of useful items within reach.
Using leftovers rather than throwing away food.
A comfortable chair and a heating pad when her back hurts.
A predictable grocery route and familiar store layout.
Practical clothing with pockets and shoes that feel stable.
A low-key family meal where no one expects her to entertain all evening.
Local neighborhood events that she can attend briefly and leave when tired.
A good bargain on something she already needed.
Simple television programs she can follow without concentrating on every line.
A clear calendar on the refrigerator that shows caregiving shifts.
Being asked for help rather than being told that she is responsible for it.
A small laugh during a stressful conversation.
Having her concerns acknowledged without someone immediately trying to reassure her.
dislikes: Food that is unexpectedly hot, pungent, or strongly seasoned.
Slimy, gritty, or unfamiliar food textures.
Complicated recipes that require precise timing across several dishes.
Crowded stores and echoing public spaces.
Online shopping pages with pop-ups, hidden fees, and too many nearly identical options.
Salespeople who use pressure or imply that an offer will disappear immediately.
Being asked to sign a form before anyone has explained what it means.
Technical language used to make a simple product sound more impressive.
People who mistake a question about literacy or paperwork for a lack of common sense.
Last-minute changes to her overnight caregiving schedule.
Lifting, carrying, or standing longer than her knees and back can tolerate.
Being told to exercise more without anyone considering pain, access, or fatigue.
A noisy phone app that sends reminders she did not ask for.
Wasteful packaging and household items that are difficult to store.
Strong perfume in a small room.
Being hurried through a decision involving money or health.
Promises from a company that do not match what happens when she asks for help.
Political conversations that turn into insults rather than discussion.
People who assume a household with a decent income has no financial worries.
An outing that has no clear plan, easy seating, or way to leave early.

other_interests_and_noninterests.reading: She does not identify reading as a hobby. She reads short practical messages, familiar recipes, labels, and selected instructions when she needs to, but does not seek out novels or long nonfiction.
other_interests_and_noninterests.pets: She does not identify animals or pets as an interest. She lives with an older indoor cat, Mabel, and handles ordinary feeding and litter tasks when her pain permits, but does not seek pet-related activities.
other_interests_and_noninterests.video_gaming: She does not identify video gaming as an interest and has not developed a habit of playing games on a console or computer.
other_interests_and_noninterests.outdoor_activities: She does not identify outdoor recreation as a hobby. She may sit on a porch or take a short level walk when her knee feels manageable, but does not choose hiking, camping, or vigorous outdoor activities for leisure.
