Uses a smartphone, web browser, maps, online banking, and common messaging apps for daily tasks, though he is not an advanced computer user.
Can compare ordinary consumer prices and read customer reviews without assuming that the highest-rated item is always the best choice.

Has basic home-maintenance abilities, such as changing filters, assembling simple furniture, and using common household tools; he calls a professional for work involving serious electrical, plumbing, or structural risks.
Is attentive to a young child’s ordinary routines, moods, food preferences, and safety needs, while recognizing that he is a parent rather than a trained clinician.
Can explain a disagreement calmly when he has had time to think about it.
Reads everyday news and practical guidance, identifies the main point, and knows when an unfamiliar topic requires more careful checking.
Knows how to ask for clarification when instructions are unclear, though embarrassment sometimes makes him wait longer than he should.

relationships.name: Grace McAllister
relationships.description: A family physician whose clinical work provides most of the household’s earned income. Her shifts and responsibilities can be demanding, so the couple coordinates schedules carefully. Evan respects her competence but sometimes worries that she carries too much emotional strain from work. They disagree about politics and spending in small ways, but tend to talk through major decisions rather than treat disagreement as a crisis.

relationships.name: Nora McAllister
relationships.description: A lively preschool-age child who is still learning to manage transitions and express what she wants. Evan is her primary daytime caregiver. He takes pleasure in familiar routines with her but also finds the repetitive, interrupted nature of childcare tiring.

relationships.name: Linda McAllister
relationships.description: Lives within a reasonable driving distance and checks in regularly. She is a committed Protestant and is more socially conservative than Evan on some issues. Their conversations are affectionate but can become careful around politics; she is proud of his caregiving even when she occasionally offers unsolicited advice.

relationships.name: Mark McAllister
relationships.description: A practical, mechanically minded man who has spent much of his life in hands-on work. Evan calls him for advice about tools, vehicles, and repairs, though both can be stubborn about whether a job needs a professional.

relationships.name: Tyler McAllister
relationships.description: Works locally and has a busier social life than Evan. They exchange brief messages and see each other more often at family gatherings than by making formal plans. Tyler jokes that Evan has become the household logistics department.

relationships.name: Church and community acquaintances
relationships.description: A small circle from their Protestant congregation and nearby community. Evan is friendly but not deeply involved in church leadership. He is more comfortable helping with a concrete task than attending a long social event without a clear purpose.

relationships.name: The McAllister family dog
relationships.description: A mixed-breed rescue dog that is part of the household. Evan enjoys the dog’s company and takes care of feeding and routine needs, though he does not treat dog ownership as a substitute for other relationships.

Clara Whitaker.nationality: American; a United States citizen by birth.

occupation.title: Not applicable; infant and not employed.
occupation.organization: None.
occupation.description: Clara does not work, earn wages, perform household labor, or participate in the labor force. Her labor-force status is nonparticipation because she is an infant, not because she is unemployed or seeking work. Her mother is the household's employed adult.

preferences.developmental_note: These are provisional sensory and routine preferences reported by caregivers, not independent consumer choices or articulate opinions. They can change quickly as Clara develops.
interests: Watching Erin's face while Erin talks to her.
Listening to familiar songs repeated with the same rhythm.
Board books with large pictures and sturdy pages.
Reaching for soft cloth toys.
Watching sunlight move across a wall from her play mat.
Exploring safe teethers with her hands and mouth.
Playing brief peekaboo games with familiar adults.
Listening to the sound of water during bath time.
Watching people prepare food from a high chair or safe nearby position.
Rolling or shifting to reach a toy placed just outside her immediate grasp.
Seeing other babies at childcare, even when she mostly watches them.
Hearing a familiar caregiver sing while changing or dressing her.
Handling textured fabric squares under supervision.
Looking at family photographs when an adult names familiar people.
Being carried outside to look at trees and passing cars.
Listening to the steady hum of ordinary home activity.
Dropping a light toy and watching an adult retrieve it.
Playing with a crinkly cloth book.
Receiving attention during calm, face-to-face play.
Exploring soft finger foods while an adult remains close.
likes: A familiar voice speaking close by, especially when the speaker gives her time to respond with a sound or look.
Being picked up with a little warning rather than abruptly lifted while she is absorbed in play.
A predictable lullaby that she has heard during several bedtime routines.
Looking at high-contrast pictures in board books.
Gentle rocking when she is tired, though it is not a guaranteed way to settle her.
Soft cotton clothing without scratchy tags near her neck.
A warm bath when she is not already overtired.
Short games of peekaboo with Erin or her grandmother.
Watching an adult smile back after she makes an excited sound.
The familiar sequence of changing, pajamas, feeding, and a quiet story at bedtime.
Small tastes of smooth oatmeal and mashed banana when she is in the mood to eat.
Soft, ripe pieces of food offered safely and closely supervised.
A teether chilled in the refrigerator, not frozen solid.
Being carried through the apartment while Erin narrates what they are doing.
A calm room after a noisy childcare pickup.
A clean, dry diaper and the chance to move freely on a safe floor mat.
A familiar blanket touching her during a supervised cuddle, but not placed loose in her sleep space.
Watching her grandmother make exaggerated expressions during play.
The quiet rustle of pages while an adult reads.
Having a trusted caregiver nearby while she explores a new toy.
dislikes_or_common_sources_of_distress: A sudden blender or vacuum noise can startle her and make her look for Erin.
Being kept in a wet or dirty diaper for longer than necessary makes her increasingly fussy.
A cold wipe against her skin can prompt a sharp protest during a change.
Being hurried through dressing when she is already tired often leads to squirming and crying.
A bright light directed toward her face bothers her more than ordinary daylight.
Being passed among several unfamiliar adults without time to observe them can overwhelm her.
A long delay between hunger cues and feeding can turn quiet fussing into crying.
A toy being taken away mid-exploration may prompt an immediate complaint, even if another toy is offered.
Overtiredness can make her resist the very rocking or feeding that usually helps.
Crowded, echoing indoor spaces can leave her quiet and watchful.
Strong fragrances around her face are avoided by her caregivers because she seems uncomfortable with them.
Scratchy seams or bulky clothing can make her wriggle and tug at the fabric.
Being laid down immediately after a lively interaction can prompt a brief protest.
A sudden change in the usual bedtime sequence can make settling take longer.
She is not fond of every purée and may clamp her mouth or turn away when she has had enough.
She dislikes having her hands restrained for longer than a necessary safety or care task.
When a stranger leans close too quickly, she may avert her gaze and become tense.
She can become frustrated when she can see a toy but cannot yet reach it.
A loud television in the background competes with the quiet interaction she responds to better.
She sometimes objects to being placed in her car seat, even though she settles once the car is moving.

personality.developmental_caveat: These are tentative descriptions of Clara's observable infant temperament, not fixed adult personality traits. Her reactions vary with hunger, sleep, illness, unfamiliar settings, and the particular caregiver present.
traits: She is observant and will sometimes watch an unfamiliar object for several seconds before reaching for it.
She is socially responsive with familiar adults, especially when they copy her sounds or pause to let her take a turn.
She shows a determined streak when a desired toy is just beyond reach, trying several movements before asking for help with a louder sound.
She can be cautious in new settings, taking time to settle rather than immediately engaging with everyone.
She is playful when rested and likes repeated games whose rhythm she recognizes.
She is sensitive to sudden loud noises, though a familiar caregiver's calm voice often helps her recover.
She has a variable tolerance for transitions and may protest when a pleasant activity ends abruptly.
She is curious about ordinary household activity and frequently watches adults moving around the room.
She can be soothed by rocking or quiet contact, but does not accept every soothing method equally every time.
She is expressive through her face and body, with visible excitement, frustration, uncertainty, and fatigue.
She can remain absorbed in a simple toy or song, but her attention is brief and easily redirected by a more interesting sound.
She is beginning to show preferences while still relying completely on adults to interpret and meet her needs.

big_five.openness: Not validly measurable as an adult trait at this age. In everyday observations, Clara shows age-typical curiosity about new sounds and objects but may first watch unfamiliar people from the safety of a familiar caregiver.
big_five.conscientiousness: Not meaningfully measurable in an infant. She has no independent planning or self-discipline; any apparent persistence is a developing motor and temperament pattern, not adult conscientiousness.
big_five.extraversion: Not meaningfully measurable as a stable adult trait. She is more vocal and interactive with familiar people and often quieter while taking in a new environment.
big_five.agreeableness: Not meaningfully measurable as a moral or adult social trait. She sometimes cooperates with familiar caregiving routines and sometimes resists them, especially when tired or interrupted.
big_five.neuroticism: Not meaningfully measurable as a stable adult trait. She has ordinary infant distress and sensitivity to fatigue, separation, and loud sounds, with recovery often supported by responsive care.

beliefs.clara: Clara has no articulated religious, political, culinary, financial, or social beliefs. She is developing basic expectations through repeated experience, such as learning which voices and routines are familiar; these are not considered convictions.
caregiver_context: Erin believes a baby's crying is communication rather than misbehavior, while recognizing that she cannot always identify the cause immediately.
Erin believes a predictable routine helps Clara feel settled, but she does not expect every day to follow the clock precisely.
Erin believes affection should be shown freely and does not worry that comforting a crying infant will spoil her.
Erin believes safe sleep practices matter even when a looser arrangement might appear more convenient.
Erin believes children should be introduced to varied foods without being pressured to finish every serving.
Erin prefers familiar home foods but is willing to offer new tastes gradually and in an age-appropriate form.
Erin thinks spicy adult food can be part of family meals later, but Clara should not be given food that is unsafe for her age.
Erin values regular pediatric care and would rather ask a clinician about a worrying symptom than rely on internet anecdotes alone.
Erin believes everyday activity and outdoor time are useful, but an infant's day should not be turned into a fitness program.
Erin thinks sleep matters for the whole household and tries to protect a calm bedtime without treating a difficult night as a failure.
Erin believes that a product marketed as organic is not automatically worth a higher price for every household purchase.
Erin checks labels for age suitability, choking hazards, and recalls before buying toys or feeding products.
Erin is open to trying a new practical baby product if it solves a real problem, but dislikes subscriptions and exaggerated claims.
Erin prefers to see a car seat or other safety equipment reviewed by a reliable source before purchasing it.
Erin shops online for predictable basics when it saves time, but buys urgent items at a nearby store.
Erin watches the household budget and will choose a conventional product that works over an expensive premium version without a clear benefit.
Erin believes a child should encounter family traditions without being required to perform them for other people's approval.
Erin wants Clara to know her extended family stories while leaving room for Clara to decide what those stories mean to her later.
Erin sees books and songs as pleasant parts of everyday life, not as a contest to make Clara advanced.
Erin believes screens should not replace holding, talking, floor play, or sleep routines for a baby.
Erin uses a phone for logistics and family photographs but tries not to leave videos playing as constant background noise.
Erin thinks childcare should be safe, affectionate, and communicative, even if it cannot imitate the exact routine at home.
Erin believes caregivers deserve clear instructions and respectful communication rather than being treated as interchangeable babysitters.
Erin values her own work because it pays the bills and gives her adult contact, even though arranging childcare can be stressful.
Erin believes reliable public services, parks, libraries, and clinics make city life more livable for families.
Erin thinks travel can broaden a child's experiences eventually, but a baby does not need frequent expensive trips.
Erin prefers short, manageable outings with Clara over ambitious plans that ignore naps and feeding.
Erin believes family financial security comes from steady habits and some luck, not from pretending that every expense is controllable.
Erin is willing to accept help from her mother, while trying to keep decisions about Clara's daily care with herself.
Erin believes Clara should be allowed to develop at her own pace and that comparison with another baby is usually unhelpful.

skills: Turns toward familiar voices and several everyday household sounds.
Uses babbling, squeals, crying, gaze, and reaching to signal needs and interest, though adults must interpret these signals in context.
Reaches for nearby toys and increasingly adjusts her body to get closer to objects.
Transfers some light toys between hands and explores them through touch and mouthing.
Recognizes familiar caregivers and often responds differently to them than to unfamiliar adults.
Participates in brief back-and-forth vocal play when a caregiver pauses and responds to her sounds.
Shows emerging ability to sit with support or briefly without it, varying with fatigue and attention.
Enjoys simple cause-and-effect play, such as dropping an object and noticing that an adult returns it.
Tolerates short periods of supported play at childcare and can be comforted by familiar staff.
Has no professional, academic, financial, cooking, shopping, or independent travel skills; those activities are managed by adults.

relationships.name: Erin Whitaker
relationships.relationship: Mother and primary caregiver. Erin works full time as a hospital billing coordinator, manages Clara's appointments and childcare arrangements, and is affectionate but sometimes tired and pressed for time.

relationships.name: Daniel Reed
relationships.relationship: Father. He and Erin were never married and do not live together. He has regular contact and planned visits; Clara is familiar with him but remains too young to describe the relationship in words.

relationships.name: Denise Whitaker
relationships.relationship: Maternal grandmother, living a short drive away. She sometimes provides backup childcare and enjoys singing to Clara, though Erin and Denise do not agree on every practical parenting choice.

relationships.name: Maya Patel
relationships.relationship: Childcare lead teacher. She knows Clara's typical feeding and nap cues and communicates practical updates to Erin at pickup.

relationships.name: Other children at childcare
relationships.relationship: Regularly present in Clara's daily environment. At this age these are familiar peers to observe and share space with, not friends in the older-child sense.
